review_body:
I felt inclined to write a review because I don't think this tacker is getting the love it deserves. It's super well built. Solid, great handle, grippy and thick. Well balanced, and easy to load. It takes generic stapes (don't have to buy the Bostitch brand if you don't want to.) All hammer tackers jam so the real issue is how easily it is to CLEAR the jam. With this one, all you do is squeeze it and take out the pin which is on the left side of the handle, remove the staples, re-load and put the pin back and you are back to work. It seems like the other reviewers did not know how to do this. That being said, I have had minimal jams. Tip: if you swing it and a staple doesn't shoot, stop and squeeze it, because it will probably drop out and you can clear it without taking it apart. However, if you keep swinging, you will make the jam worse and take more time to clear it out.

Overall, great tacker! I love this thing. Got it for 19.99 at Lowes and I would suggest others do the same.

product_title: Woodstock Tool Table
review_headline: You get what you pay for, somewhat
review_body:
As others mentioned, this stand suffers from material and workmanship deficiencies. The steel components are poorly formed in places and holes do not always line up, requiring some creative assembly techniques. The top is somewhat as described, a "butcher block finish" consisting of low density pressed paper covered with contact paper - I wouldn't even call it MDF.

That said, I am not completely unhappy with the purchase since it was quite inexpensive. I would not be happy if I had paid more. I would not recommend this to someone with limited experience in making things work.

I am using it with a heavy Rikon 6x48"/10" belt/disc sander and so far it is sturdy, without wobble or shake after a few weeks of sanding. I don't think I would use it with casters without adding extra reinforcement, for example a stiffening plywood shelf. Also, my sander had a big enough footprint that I was able to fasten some bolts through the upper steel brackets which probably helped. The safest thing for general use may be to toss the paper top and make one from plywood.

Some tips. When assembling the frame the bolt holes are difficult to line up in places, especially on the upper brackets. This is far easier with a drift pin, standard industry practice. I used a sturdy awl I had ground from an old screwdriver to force the holes onto alignment. I've used this on plenty of other assemblies including things I've built from scratch. Make sure ALL the bolts are kept loose until the end after setting the stand upright on a level surface. I tighten all moderately then retighten. The included bolts seem undersized to me and low quality so don't over-tighten.

When drilling holes for the top be careful of the bit selection. This is important when putting screws into any pressed fiber board products and especially with this low quality top. If the drill bit is too big the screws will easily strip and not hold - if the bit is too small the pressboard will probably split. The bit size should closely match the screw shaft not including the threads. One trick with crumbly materials is to squirt a bit of wood glue into the hole before tightening he screw. In any case, don't over-tighten!

Since the steel is not a very heavy gauge, stiffening the entire stand with a plywood shelf might be a good thing if used with a planer or some tool stressed with heavy boards or having significant vibration. Also, a heavy tool with a narrow footprint might benefit from adding some reinforcement to pressboard top in the short dimension since the maker failed to (or simply make a sturdy plywood top)

Overall I'm satisfied with the stand and might even buy another one if the price is ever reduced to make up for the extra assembly effort and possible modifications needed. It is certainly functional for my application and less effort than cutting angle iron and making a sturdier stand from scratch, although assembly by welding would be far quicker than with all those screws.too small the pressboard will probably split. product_title: Bosch GMS120 Digital Multi-Scanner
review_headline: The perfomance in the field had too many problems to make it useful
review_body:
I'm sure this looked great on the drawing board, but the performance in the field had so many problems that it made it almost useless. It was way too sensitive. The slightest uneven or rough surface would cause it to indicate that there was a stud - the surface had to be perfectly flat to get an acurate reading. For example, I was trying to find a stud on a tiled shower wall and the tiles were not perfectly flat-every time I moved from one tile to the next, it would indicate that there was a stud.
Another problem I had was the fact that you can not turn off the metal detecting or electric current detecting ability. All of the detectors are on when you have it on stud finding. I have aluminum siding on my house so when trying to find a stud on an outside wall the metal detector would be on constantly - which meant that the red indicator light and audible alarm would be on constantly as well. Pretty much making the indicators useless because you couldn't rely either to indicate when you actually moved over a stud.
The things I liked about the bosch was the fact that the metal detector worked really well (that's how I ended up finding the studs on the shower wall, by detecting the nails used to affix the sheetrock to the stud- not the most acurate method but it worked). I also liked the fact that you didn't have to continuously press the on button (as it is with my other "yellow" stud finder - I'm sure you know what brand). One touch on, one touch off - nice feature. In perfect conditions the features worked great, but how often do you encounter perfect conditions in real life?

Overall this was a big zero. The problems with sensitivity made it virtually useless.

product_title: Vega PRO 50 Table Saw Fence System: 42-Inch Fence Bar, 50-Inch to Right
review_headline: Easy to install once you see video
review_body:
I have a Craftsman 10\\" with a 27\\" deep table, and on the left is an extension with a router mounted so I wanted the fence to go clear to the left side. I also have a small shop and don't have room for the rails to extend very far to the right. I researched many fences on-line as there's no place to actually see them in Oregon, and settled on Vega.

I called the Vega company and got to customer service. Randy was super helpful and recommended a Vega 40. He said I could drill and tap a couple of holes to move the rails, and recommended Amazon as the best price. He also offered to send me a replacement tape since I was moving the rails and the old one would be off.

I ordered the fence, which came on time and in good shape. When I got all the parts out and read the instructions I was a bit confused. The instructions are complete but not easy to follow. HOWEVER - there is a video made by a third party that shows the installation - [...] - and after watching that I had the fence installed in 30 minutes.

There are extra tapped holes in the front rail and a pair of them matched existing holes in the table. I had to drill one hole in the back of the table to match the back rail. I got the old tape off with Acetone and the new tape when on easily. I now have a bit over 30\\" to the right of the blade and can use the fence with the router on the left - just what I wanted.

A HINT: be sure to put any facing you want on the fence before putting on the new tape. I added 3/4' and then matched up the tape.

Also, with my old fence I had to push the locking handle down hard to lock - not with the Vega. It locks with little effort. Some WD40 makes it slide easily. I'm a happy new user.

product_title: BAFX Products (TM) - Pack of 5 - Super Bright - Aluminum - 9 LED Flashlights W/ Carrying Strap
review_headline: (too many) FAILURES in MANUFACTURE - but company will correct problems
review_body:
THIRD REVIEW (2 stars - February 2, 2014):
As mentioned earlier, one unit came w/o half its connectors - which I fixed with some aluminum foil. Then I had to force the inner spring, attached to the LED array component inside the tube, to the middle on another unit enough so that it would make better contact and work.

Sadly, gradually ALL of the flashlights have failed due to what I see, I think, is a very BAD systemic error. To wit, EVERY ONE OF THE SPRINGS soldered to the front of the tube are very noticeably offset making for an unreliable contact with batter array contact. This spring is totally inaccessible after manufacture - I have tried to unscrew front LED section to get at back of the unit to maybe re-solder w/o any success.

The result is the contact between battery pack and front spring is tenuous and shifts enough at times to lose contact so light goes off. Eventually all these offset springs caused failure.

After first review below, I told the manufacturer's email checker that I was happy I had several working units for $10. Now I am not happy. I have one working reliable unit left.

These fine little flashlights are obviously made to be bomb-proof. Unfortunately, whatever robot or person(s) doing the critical soldering of the spring to the LED section is doing a horrible job. Actually, I think the design of that section is bad to begin with because there is too little space to properly solder the spring perfectly centrally w/o getting in the way of something else and shorting a circuit. That's all I can tell.

.....................................

SECOND REVIEW (4 stars): - I originally gave these 3 stars and thought maybe I was slightly generous. But within hours of posting my review, the company emailed me through Amazon asking if they could help me get all I paid for - new working units or repairs or something. So I give them back 1 star for trying unusually hard to do right. I would buy again knowing the company stands behind their product. However ...

SUGGESTION: (which I'll send back to the company as well as posting here)
\\"Spend $.50 per unit extra for quality control and then charge $2.50 for these otherwise excellent little flashlights. It is inexcusable for there to be lapses in quality control but maybe you are thinking you have to cut operations to the bone. You don't! I think there IS a market out there for your specified product, which I think is somewhere between disposable cheap toy-like junk so many others produce and twice or more as expensive flashlights that are also available. Your price point, once you get quality control in hand, I think could be $2.50 per unit. I'd be glad to pay that for a serious product like you seem to want to sell. Just get the quality control in hand! I bet you can buy a LOT of quality control for fifty cents extra per unit. Maybe for half that. I'd think so, anyway.\\"

........................

product_title: Uvex S345C Futura Safety Goggles, Clear Frame, Clear Uvextreme Anti-Fog Lens, Indirect Vent, Neoprene Headband
review_body:
These glasses were mandatory for my General Chemistry, both as a student and as an assistant, and I can tell you that they are the most unbearable things in the world. As a Chemistry major, it is not uncommon for me to wear the glasses for up to 8 hours a day, most of the week, so here are just a few of the problems that I have noticed after long use.

To begin with, the elastic band likes to slip out of the plastic adjusters. In fact, I got so angry with these goggles in lab once that I re-strung the band and superglued the excess in place. At least not they don't spontaneously expand.

Second, the plastic seal that makes contact with your face is really sharp. Not only do you leave lab with the expected goggle lines, sometimes you leave with bleeding scratches. For this I got in the habit of smearing Vaseline around the edge of the goggles. It seems to help, but now my face is greasy.

Lastly, and worst of all, the lenses scratch and fog up very quickly. After about five minutes they have to be removed and wiped dry. Obviously this is not acceptable. When I cleaned my goggles, I only used soft cloths, like one would use on reading glasses, but within a week of purchase, I noticed scratches in my field of view.

I would not buy these glasses again. It might be worth the fight with the Chem Department to simply get a different type of goggles.

product_title: SecurityIng SF09 600 Lumens XM-L T6 LED Adjustable Focus 5 Modes Flashlight
review_headline: Same flashlite under different brand names but Very Bright
review_body:
This flashlight is branded by different manufacturers engraving their own name on the it's body (Ultrafire, Windfire, SecurityIng, etc . . .). But I think they are all made by one company. At the time of this review Price varies from $6.00 to $30.00, depending on the engraved name. However, based on reviews (from generic to known brand names of this flashlight, with CREE XM-L T6 LED emitter), I decided to go with $10.00 - $15.00 price range & this review is for one with SecurityIng brand.

This flashlight is very bright, much brighter than my 250 Lumens. However, I seriously doubt if it is 1600 Lumens. It is twice brighter than my 250L, but definitely not 5 or 6 times brighter. I am getting sufficient light with 3 x AAA batteries & I have not run this flashlight with 18650 type batteries yet, but I am sure it will be brighter. Even with AAA batteries the light is so bright that it may damage the eyes if you try to loo into the flashlight directly.
Despite impressive amount of light that it produces, when zoomed in, the light becomes square shape rather than circle. The more you zoom in, the more square shape the light will be at the end. Beside the square shape light, the location of the button at the tail of flashlight is not that convenient & it is not as quick as button on the side to turn off & on.
Overall is a bright & stylish flashlight outperforming many more expensive ones, but if you get it below $15.00, it is worth it, but not more than that.

Update 02-02-2014:
I finally got a chance to get my hands on 18650 Batteries (3200mAh) & compare the output of this flashlight with some higher end flashlights.
1st: The amount of light produced with 18650 battery is at least twice brighter than 3 x AAA batteries.
2nd: This flash light at its best is 250 to 350 Lumens (with 18650) & 60 to 70 Lumen with 3xAAA.

I compared this to my Sunwayman D04a, which is a true 960 Lumen Flashlight. While it may not be two comparable flashlights ($80 vs. $12.00 flashlight), but the brightness of lights were the focus. The brightness of SecurityIng Flashlight is about four times less than my Sunwayman. So the rule of thumb applied here again:
\\"The cheaper the flashlight, the more inflated lumen presented by manufacturer\\".
Despite above, still plenty of light for flashlight at this price.

product_title: Eastwood 12012 Mig Welder with Spool Gun, 175 Amp, 220VAC, 10 Pack
review_headline: 175 Arrived Damaged. Spool Gun (motor) defective. Being returned.
review_body:
I ordered the Eastwood MIG 175 + Spool Gun + Cart combo kit.

The MIG 175 arrived carrier-damaged (thanks FedEx). The front-left-bottom corner completely crushed in. In Eastwood's defense, the shipping box is wonderfully packaged and reasonably thick. But I guess not thick enough.

I attempted to play with the spool gun anyhow. Imagine my surprise that when you press the trigger, the wires is pushed back towards the spool. Assuming the wires soldered to the drive motor were backwards, I went to Google to verify. Though I couldn't find any specific posts to Eastwood products, other spool gun purchasers have had this problem. FWIW, the drive motor on the welder itself (for carbon wire) spins correctly...

I called Eastwood directly for the return (purchased there instead of here on Amazon) and the rep admitted they received a bad batch in (presumably from China). There was minor flack with the rep about who was paying return postage, but when I stated it was damaged, the flack went away.

The 175 is trashed and is being returned today. The spool gun is going with it.

I use a dozen Eastwood products regularly (powder coating gun and their powders), but this welder purchase left a sour taste in my mouth. Going with Hobart and we'll see how that goes.

I can't thoroughly review the welder itself since it was damaged, but visually it's sharp. Nice black powder coating on the exterior. Simple controls in the flip-up housing. The spool gun problem really frustrates me, though.

review_headline: Medium-sized shop vac provides good value.
review_body:
Excellent shop-vac for the price. It's what i'd consider on the medium-size side for shop vac, perfect for a small urban house with occasional shop-vac needs, such as my friend whose small basement happen to flood on the exact day that I received this.

Basically, it's lightweight and has all the usual shopvac attachmetns. The lightweightness means that it's not particularly "heavy duty", such as the wheels are just more or less simple wheels and not meant to go off-roading, but for most of us, that should be fine.

I also like that it's not particularly loud while providing good suction power to, as I said, clean out my friend's basement. Emptying the thing was not hard as it was smartly designed. Not that it matters too much, but it's also a smart looker as shop vacs go - it looks at first glance to be more expensive than it is. It can certainly do jobs that even today's relatively heavy-duty "inside the house" vacs cannot do.

Small negative: for storage in tight areas, it would have been nice if the black detachable handle could be installed 'reversed.' Likewise, they might have thought of a smarter solution to store the little attachment pieces.

Because of its relatively small size, this shop vac is probably not suited for heavy duty or large use. I suggest you get familiar with the volume sizes of these things before deciding whether this works for you.

Final verdict: excellent shop vac for the price. Go for it.

product_title: Jet 708718R Band Saw Rip Fence With Resaw Guide
review_headline: Does NOT fit ALL 14" Jet Bandsaws
review_body:
This product is really a problem for both the seller and the manufacturer.

I received this fence today only to find out that it does not fit my 14\\" Jet bandsaw, which was a surprise because on the side of the box it claims boldly that \\"This fence fits ALL Jet 14\\" bandsaws.\\"

The problem is that the fence itself is about 1-1/4\\" too long for the spacing between the rails. I measured my table and it is just shy of 14\\" (13-3/4\\"). The fence, therefore, is built for a table that is 15\\".

I fixed the problem using 1\\" wooden shims on the back rail and a couple of longer 1/4\\" 20 screws that were long enough to compensate for the extra depth created by the shims.

The locking system was also not working at all, but then I discovered a plastic shim in the box that had fallen off the locking tongue. I glued it on with CA glue and it's now working as it should.

In the end, after significant modifications, the fence is square, true, calibrated, functional and locks to the rail, so I'm not going to return it because it would likely be too much bother for too little gain.

But buyer beware - especially if you own a Jet bandsaw.

The profile is also more slender than conventional pliers which requires you to squeeze the handles closer together. This was not much of a problem using the plier jaws to manipulate items, but I found I had a hard time getting good leverage when using the wire cutters.
The holster is constructed of nylon mesh that is reinforced with leather in areas where extensive wear would occur. Very nice quality.
The outer shell is made of a hardened plastic that is very robust and took quite a beating without showing much wear.
The bit driver was the least useful component on this tool. The driver is set in close to the main body of the tool so the throat is actually wider than the bit, making it a pain to get into tight areas and keeping it lined up with the fastener. Using an extension would fix this problem, but, sadly, the tool does not come with its own extension. I found myself grabbing a conventional driver more often than not.
While this tool will not replace my leatherman multi-tool as my “everyday tool”. It has certainly found a spot in my tackle box as the pliers and blade are ideal for fishing trips.

product_title: Drill Press Laser Guide
review_body:
Works very nicely.

Setup / alignment needs care but produces good results.

I mounted the unit to the cast boss where the drill head attaches to the pillar as this was slightly larger and fitted the hose-pipe clip better. The focus on the lines is better at the slightly larger distance too.

Align each laser vertically first using the supplied tool (cover one laser then the other to avoid distractions). To adjust slacken the 2 Allen headed screws and adjust the laser lens head assembly - tighten and check as you go !

Then rotate each complete unit to align the cross point after slacking off each top thumb screw. Lock everything off.

The cross produced on my unit is very accurate indeed.

The plastic at the back where the clip exits the unit and then goes around the pillar will break when you tighten it if the pillar is smaller than the said plastic piece - beware.

My pillar was smaller than the unit (pillar 70mm : 2 3/4in) but the cast boss on the head was just the right size (80mm) and the unit fitted using the smaller hose-pipe clip as supplied. The clip does have to be well tightened to provide a good wobble free mounting.

I sharpened one chisel (1/4-inch round nose scraper) and used it with reasonable success. I was quite satisfied with that -- I can make some nice new handles and a better case if I think that is necessary. Unfortunately, all four other chisels were bent. Or inserted crookedly into the handles. I applied moderate pressure on the 1/8-inch spindle gouge, using a single finger, to see if the chisel would move in the handle. The chisel snapped off clean, about 1/4-inch in front of the handle! It just snapped clean off when I pressed on it with one finger!

Yes, these chisels are cheap and you get what you pay for. But I paid for woodturning chisels and these should have been fit for that task to at least some reasonable degree.

One out of five chisels useable. One out of five stars.

product_title: Black & Decker HG1300 Dual Temperature Heat Gun
review_body:
I got this heat gun to have in my home tool kit. It works great and is of good quality.

Here are some of the main uses for a heat gun that I have personally tried:

1. Shrink Wrapping. You can also use a hair dryer for this, but this gun works better and faster.
2. Drying Paint. If you need to speed up the drying of paint, this will do it.
3. Paint Stripping. You can use this gun to avoid using toxic chemicals to strip paint off of furniture or woodwork (there are articles and videos on the Internet to show how).
4. Soften Adhesives. This is great for removing stickers from your windshield or old bumperstickers. Just heat the sticker with the heat gun and then easily peel it off. Any remaining glue residue can be removed non-toxically by rubbing it with any kind of oil, including regular old cooking oil, then scrubbing with a cloth or paper towel.

Safety Warnings:

1. Be careful to not obstruct or cover the air inlet grills because this could cause the heat gun to overheat and, worst case, catch fire.
2. Don't put the nozzle of the gun right on top of anything. It can have the same dangerous effect as Item 1.
3. Don't use the heat gun near anything flammable.
4. Don't put down the gun without turning it off.
5. Don't store the gun until it has fully cooled.
6. Don't touch the hot metal nozzle to your skin (it can burn you) or your clothing (it can set it on fire).
7. Don't use this heat gun to strip lead-based paint--it can release dangerous fumes.
8. Do not look directly into the nozzle when the gun is turned on--it could harm your eyes.
9. Do not insert anything into the nozzle of the gun, it could overheat the gun and be a fire hazard and/or damage the gun.

review_headline: Note: Min/Max feature does not include Average
review_body:
This meter seems to be a quality meter that performs as advertised. One point to be aware of is that the Min/Max feature on this meter is more limited than on many other Fluke products. The Min/Max feature does NOT give Average values. While it does not claim to do so, Fluke does a very poor job of differentiating between Min/Max and Min/Max/Avg on their product description pages.

In short, if you need average voltage or current, you will need to look at a different product.

review_headline: Installed in Surefire G2 Nitrolon, Fits perfectly
review_body:
Do yourself a favor and toss out that crap incandescent bulb in the Surefire G2 and step up to real power.

Just kidding but, the difference is astounding. If you wanted a bright light and ended up with a G2 Nitrolon because of price (Hey, I understand), then add this bulb and get everything that you already expected plus dramatically extended battery life! The light is pretty "white" but for the price, I consider it a compromise that I'm willing to make. All things being equal, I would have just bought another flashlight in the first place in lieu of bulb replacement but, I already had the light (as I suspect that you do too).

I did stick one of these in a Streamlight Protac that I have and, while the diode doesn't extend in to the reflector perfectly, the shape of the reflector and body naturally center the diode and it works like a champ. I have the factory LED version of the Protac and this is just as bright and the beam is just as focused. I'm not recommending it but, it worked for me. It saves me on replacing the CR123A batteries all the time as well.

product_title: PowerSmith PAVC101 10 Amp Ash Vacuum
review_headline: I've melted almost every piece of this thing
review_body: We heat our home exclusively with a free standing wood stove. I purchased this vacuum with the idea that I could vacuum out the ash instead of shoveling it out and greatly reduce the dust in my home.  I realized that this vacuum nor any other was designed to suck the firebox clean of hot coals and have not tried to do that.  Ash is hot, and this is a hot ash vacuum.  The first thing that somehow melted was a little \\"cage\\" that keeps the filter away from the motor, that melted and now the motor sucks the filter directly against it and literally destroys the filter almost immediately.  The hose is made of metal and coated with a rubbery plastic on the outside, which is now melted off in several spots.  When I use it I either let the fire burn out or if its a super cold day I let it burn way down and move the coals off to one side and vacuum up the ash.  I actually have a metal kitty litter scoop that I use to separate the coals from the ash so I don't accidently suck one up.  Still this thing is basically destroyed already, I took it out to the garage and \\"retired\\" it as it is no longer usable to me.  With the filter unable to hold up it spews ash out the top \\"out\\" port and all over my house.  I've looked all over for \\"warnings\\" that say the way I'm using it is wrong but I don't see any.  From what I read I'm using it how it is advertised to be used.  I see that it has a 2 year warranty so I'm going to find my paperwork and see if they will stand behind it or just tell me I sucked up something too hot and it was my fault.  I will update this when this is resolved.

product_title: Bayco SL-825 13-Watt Fluorescent Work Light with 40-Feet Cord Reel
review_headline: Poor Product and Defective Upon Receipt
review_body: This item was defective upon receipt and is of poor quality.  The shipping box from Amazon was fine and in good solid condition but inside the bubble wrap the product  box from the manufacturer was not.  The product box was partially open and looked fairly battered.  All it was missing to complete the picture was some duct tape holding the hapless product package together.  Without knowing anything my first thought was that it looked like the item might have been bought, opened, used, returned and then resent to me.  Not sure if this was the case but I immediately plugged it in and the lamp did not work.  I remembered several other reviews stating the lamp assembly was flimsy and prone to flickering and failure.  I unplugged the cord, opened the fluorescent tube housing at the top and adjusted the bulb.  I plugged it back in and the light flickered on briefly.  After several attempts to seat the tube the light simply would not stay on for more than a second or two and then go out with the slightest movement.  Clearly the other reviews that the light socket for the tube/bulb on this product is of poor quality and prone to shorts were spot on accurate.  Strangely enough the other elements of the product and design seemed to be quite sturdy.  Seems odd that they splurged on everything else with this product but then fit the most critical element, the light, with such a poor quality socket which is clearly susceptible to immediate failure.  I returned the product within five minutes of opening the box (Amazon promptly accepted the return) and will not be buying anything from Bayco again.

review_body: After reading the reviews on this too.  I decided to get it.  This tool is a hand cramp SAVER.  I was using a manual caulk gun for polyurethane caulk for sealing around my window frames. The hand squeezing the gun would start to cramp up due to the amount of squeeze force needed to get the caulking to flow out.  I could only last laying down about 18" to 24" before I had to stop and rest my hand.  On top of this, my bead was not consistently even!  I hooked the air gun to my Porter Cable 6 gallon pancake compressor rated at 135 psi and did not need to use the air regulator included with this gun.  I was using about 90 psi (recommend max psi per manufacturer) and the caulking was flowing smoothly and stopped flowing when I released the trigger.  Initially, I thought the gun was not working because it was bleeding (air) when I pulled the trigger and nothing was coming out.  Eventually, the caulking made it up the nozzle and out.  I was able to caulk six windows and a consistent bead in way less time than caulking one window using a manual gun.

I've had it less than a week, but already have done 3 projects in my garage with its help, thus far. When I'm done with it, it folds quickly and takes up very little space between my work bench and tool cabinet. One thing I'd recommend to anyone who purchases the product on-line is to go to '[...] and print the on-line instruction manual so that it is on-hand when your Folding Work Table arrives. The manual is well illustrated and helpful in describing how best to set up, fold down, and use the clamping features of the Table. I like the 'Keter' Folding Work Table so much, that I'm tempted to get another for my wife to use in her sewing room for big projects she works on. Thank you, 'Keter'.

product_title: Denali Miter Saw Stand
review_headline: Very sturdy and easy to setup.
review_body:
This product is well made, very sturdy, and thus heavy. Due to it's weight, this stand would benefit greatly from a set of casters on one end of the frame so that it can be more easily moved when folded.

Overall design is very good. The leg hinges and button locks seem pretty sturdy. There are a few plastic pieces and the plastic seems to be of cheap quality, allowing easy damage. My stand had minor damage to the plastic end caps, and one of the plastic covers on the saw quick mounts was broken upon delivery. Since it wasnt a critical component, and the quick connect braces work, I didnt worry about it.

The end brackets that attach to the arms and support rollers are not labeled and the instructions are not clear as to how they should be attached, leaving it up to the end user to figure out the best way to attach them so that the rollers line up with the saw. When I setup my stand, I attached the brackets so the rollers would be to the inside of the extension arms, which aligns the rollers pretty well. The roller heights are easily adjustable, and the arms extend pretty far.

The height of the stand is not adjustable, but is a comfortable height for me (6'0\\").

One of the support rollers was delivered with a fairly large rust spot. I have not yet contacted Amazon about this issue.

Overall, I am very satisfied with this stand, which is my first.

review_headline: Grip is excellent, adhesion is useless
review_body:
The surface grip of the product is excellent. This part should last some time. It was easy to cut lengths with a scissors. The problem is the adhesion to the intended surface you want to make non-slip. In my application I was applying strips to a sheet of sandply plywood that had been stained. I was making a indoor wheelchair ramp from the garage into the house for my neighbor. By the time I had the 3rd strip down the 1st strip was already loose at the edges. I applied 16 strips total that day and by the next morning all but 4 were coming up. Decided to re-stick them down and give it a test by running a leaf blower over the ramp from about 15 feet away. When I did that all the strips came off. Since I liked the surface "grip" I decided to take another reviewer's advise and took my pneumatic upholstery stapler and stapled the strips down. Problem solved.

So surface grip good, adhesion to intended surface bad, bordering awful. There are ways around this though as posted above.

The problems:
- The lanyard string is too thin to be as useful as it could be, Replace it with paracord which you can actually use to tie something securely or separate into the multiple inner cores and the sheath, etc. I'm also not impressed with the location of the loop that leaves this hanging at an awkward angle.
- The flint stick (which does work with a good striker) is located in a way that makes it hard to throw sparks accurately. - The whistle works OK, but you have to find just the right level of breath. Too little it isn't loud, and too much and the pea jams.
- The rather small mirror has a rather tall rim around it that cuts way down on the angles you can reflect light to / from.
- The gasket quality varies - on some it's a softer material and seals well, but on just one (of several) it is just hard plastic that doesn't really help the seal at all.
- it's a bit large to pack in smaller survival kits or keep in your pocket and see above about it hanging at a somewhat awkward angle if you wear it around your neck.

The better stuff about it:
- The compasses on these have actually proven pretty stable. This is the part of this piece of kit I've used the most often.
- The whistle is OK if you get your breath strength right. It could actually be used as a sports whistle in a pinch.
- The mirror is good for getting something out of your eye (spoken from experience) or looking down the bore of a firearm.
- If you've got one with a good gasket, the match / tinder / whatever holder will keep things dry as well as any matchbox holder
- While the whistle part seems a bit fragile, I haven't actually broken it, and the rest of it seems pretty tough for being just plastic. It has survived being in a back pocket and being sat down and being tossed around a a tool box.der

product_title: DEWALT DW920K-2 1/4-Inch 7.2-Volt Cordless Two-Position Screwdriver Kit
review_body:
The DeWalt DW920K-2 is a battery powered screwdriver. Some of the things that separate it from cheaper screwdrivers are;

1) Variable speed
2) Greater torque
3) Torque control
4) Quick release chuck
5) Replaceable battery (2 supplied with charger)

This is not a drill/driver. While it can be used for relatively slow speed pre-drilling (500 rpm), don't let the dome shaped quick release collar fool you into believing it has a keyless jawed chuck. Its chuck is just a deep ¼\\" hex socket, like any other battery screwdriver, with added retention/release mechanism. You won't be able to use your round shank drill bits without a jawed chuck adapter. There are also ¼\\" hex shank drill bits available for anyone wanting to use it as a drill.

Having said that, and brushed any amount of subliminal marketing deception on the part of DeWalt under the carpet, the tool performs well within its limitations. I have both an 18V drill/driver and an impact driver and got this to replace two aging screwdrivers here. A screwdriver has obvious advantages in tight spaces but one of the annoyances I've found with those here is the lack of torque. Some mundane Ikea type furniture assembly jobs would have them stalling even when fairly new and with fully charged batteries.

The DW920K-2 did have disassembly problems with heavy machine workbenches using 3/8\\" bolts and nuts and my suggestion to anyone needing non-drill torque greater than the \\"13\\" (23 in-lbs) setting is to use a more powerful tool. This is for two reasons....1) This tool tends to stall at the \\"15\\" (25 in-lbs) setting without any clutch slip......2) Clutch slip above \\"13\\" can cause the torque adjustment collar assembly to bind afterwards for settings above \\"13\\". It will require a good amount of force to unbind the collar in order for it to rotate all the way to the drill setting again. Works fine after that.

It's always a good idea to download and read the manual for anything before purchasing. This tool is no exception and DeWalt has both user and parts manuals at their website. Those needing more torque and better cordless drilling capability may find purchasing a drill/driver, with keyless chuck, to make more sense, and there are lesser brand 18V tools to be had at around the same price point as this screwdriver.nual for anything before purchasing. product_title: DEWALT DCS380B 20-Volt MAX Li-Ion Reciprocating Saw, Bare Tool Only
review_body:
I'm a professional builder with a tendency to eschew new gimmicks and hot trends just so I can have bragging rights to the latest and greatest. If my existing tools are working and doing the job well, I'll stay loyal to them and spend the money on taking my wife to dinner. Having said that, a while back I decided it was time to come into the 21st century and upgrade my old 9V Makita system to 20V. So, I'd been using the 20V Max system for a while (love it) but didn't really see a need for the battery operated reciprocating saw as my old, corded Makita worked just fine. I confess, I was also afraid it wouldn't (couldn't?) have the real strength/power of a corded saw. Then I had a job installing a fireplace and had to go in an attic to set the chimney. Dragging a cord back and forth to where I had to cut out roof sheathing became a hassle so I decided to go for the battery operated reciprocating saw.

What a wonderful tool. Not only does it have the capacity to set your blade teeth in any of four directions (which allows you to cut closer to some obstructions) but the very shoe itself is adjustable to three different depths so you can effectively adjust the cut depth. By the way, it has power to spare!

I have not used it long enough (in one day) to vouch for battery life so I have no opinion on that. The 20V Max system has long battery life in general (a little short with the circular saw) and I love the ability to push a button and visually see how much battery is left.

My only wish: DeWalt should bring back the hard cases for their hand tools. When you pack your tools into a truck to carry to a job, the cases not only protected them but are also a big help in keeping organized. I really miss those.

review_body:
This BOSCH L-Cart is a back saving invention, that I wish had been around for the past 20 years. So many times I've hauled around big loudspeakers and keyboards, because a hauling cart (Dolly) wouldn't fit in my hatchback car. If I had this folding BOSCH L-cart, I could have moved my equipment without ruining my back. This cart can fit almost anywhere. Why? The BOSCH L-CART folds up FLAT! The design is ingenious. The handle slides down, the wheels fold flat against the back, and the bottom plate folds flat. So the whole cart is only 2 inches thick when folded, and about 32 inches high. Obviously it stores places you could NEVER place a solid cart.

When you're ready to use it, you pulled down the loading plate, pull out the wheels, which lock into position, and you press a button, and pull up the handle. Then, load up your boxes. If you're worried about stability, or the load falling off the cart, you use the orange cords that are strapped to the middle of the cart. They wrap around your load, and snap into place. I still double up (foam plugs and HL earmuffs). When you are shooting at a range, you are exposed to over 100-140 (or more) Decibels. Because I double up, I crank up the volume on my HL earmuffs and have no issues hearing what's going on around me....until someone pops of a round next to me, which is when the earmuffs kick in and I get my 30 NRR protection.

I used the unit when I was shooting rifles and had no issues with using my scope or iron sights.

Highly recommended.

product_title: Duracell Durabeam Ultra High Intensity Tactical- 500 Lumen Flashlight 2-Pack with 6 C Batteries
review_headline: Brightness drops quickly, apparently no voltage regulator in this model
review_body:
The focus control is nice, and got them for a good price at Costco.

Both ends of the flashlight are flat, so it will stand on either end. One end has five flat edges so it won't roll away either. There is no wrist strap (or any hole for one to be added).

The large push button on the end normally cycles between low/high/strobe/off, but the button is not \\"de-bounced\\" so sometimes it skips a position when pressed. With fingers wrapped around the grip, operating the push button on the end is a two-handed operation.

When focused tightly, the shape of the beam is basically rectangular, which is the shape of the CREE LED chip. When zoomed out, the flashlight projects a large circle of even brightness with no \\"spot\\" in the middle, excellent for illuminating a large area.

However, this model flashlight seems to lack a voltage regulator and brightness is therefore VERY dependent on battery voltage.

For example, at the high setting, the brightness decreases quickly (simply turn on the other flashlight to compare). After about 1 minute (using the original Duracell alkaline C cells), the brightness is about half the level it was at when first powered on. The brightness steadily decreases after that.

I also tried 1900maH Sanyo Eneloop NiMH AA batteries (with AA to C spacers), and the brightness decreased much more rapidly (as expected). The AA batteries lasted only 1 hour on \\"high\\", but after only about 10 minutes the brightness had dropped below the original \\"low\\" output level. I know that C batteries are about 3X more capacity but I don't like having to stock yet another size of rechargeable batteries so I was hoping that I could use NiMH AA's (besides the fact that NiMH cells have lower output voltage which will result in lower brightness from this flashlight, I also read that some rechargeable C batteries are really just AA's with some padding so I need to be careful to find some rechargeable C's with highest mAh capacity).

C batteries fit loosely in the flashlight tube, and rattle around when the flashlight is moved. C batteries are easily swapped out, since they're not in a separate plastic \\"battery holder\\" inside the tube. I would suggest putting some plumber's grease on the aluminum threads, since you may be replacing the batteries frequently.

If you don't need longer operating times and want to make your own AA-to-C battery adapter that's the right size for 3 cells, try a 5-7/8\\" length piece of 1/2\\" Schedule-40 PVC with a strip of fuzzy velcro taped around each end -- then the AA batteries dump out of the tube easily just like the C cells.

product_title: PortaPow USB Power Monitor / Multimeter / DC Ammeter for Solar Panels, Mains Chargers, etc
review_body:
GREAT for checking source voltage & charge amperage from any usb source.
Verify that you're getting adequate voltage & amperage in real-time.

Under 5V at the source when charging? Your charger isn't "keeping up" with your device's charging capacity.

Getting adequate USB voltage (5.0-5.5V) at the charging source, but lower-than-expected amperage (while charging)?
It MAY be caused by your charging cable. At higher charge amperages, small-gauge cable used in many USB cables (especially cheaper aftermarket cables) causes significant voltage drop at the device. Lower voltage "starves" the device, and it may not charge at its maximum rated rate.
This is especially true of USB 3.0 devices, larger smartphones & tablets.

Even under "perfect" conditions, your device may not draw maximum rated current if its battery is near 100% capacity. To make sure your charging source & cable are up-to-task, check the amperage & voltage with the device at 50% battery capacity or lower.

I did experience noise from the probe when I tried to trace the exact line among several other wires. Actually after a while I realized that I could get by with just using some telephone jacks and a line tester to figure out the wiring network.  Nevertheless, this product did simplify the id process.  Why the 2 stars?  Well on my next project, I used this same product to trace Romex wires behind drywall.  No good.  It's not powered to do so.  I ended up purchasing a Fluke wire tracer...that one is excellent!  So to summarize, I'm probably retiring this Sperry product now that I have the Fluke. review_body:
4 stars, plenty of look a like so this is probably a rebadged product.

All these complains about short battery life got me curious about my WR300. I hook up the WR300 and measured the current the unit draws 0.082mA and 0.024mA when standby at 3.0V. A typical Lithium CR2032 has a capacity of 220mAh.

So calculating the working hours of the unit

220 / 0.082 = 2682 hours = 111 days of continuous operation

220 / 0.024 = 9166 hours = 381 days of standby mode

I call it standby mode because the unit is not really off, as it has to keep the accelerometer data alive. Hence the parasitic power drain.

For me it's pretty good battery life. I don't know if this is manufacturing issue or they have updated the WR300 but if your battery life is short, I suggest that you make a warranty claim.

well here is good news the Triac BTB16 is generic and can be found on Ebay for $5 for 10 shipped. this is the most common component to fail. the next thing is R1 which I found out that is 1k, 0.25W(mine was burnt beyond recognition) so I beefed it up to 1W. I have reversed engineered the controller with schematics,PCB board and BOM. it is elementary single layer Triac/Diac(32v) circuit... very simple. review_body:
This is the only cutter I have, that is precise enough to cut paper. My other ones, will not make a cut along the entire length of the blade, as the alignment isn't as precise.
It uses standard sized utility knife blades, which is good as they are cheap and easy to find, but it does limit the size of what you can cut. If you don't need to cut anything bigger than a garden hose in one snip, they will be just fine. They will cut larger hoses, if you 'squash' it, cut from one side, and then the other.
Probably the best feature (other than the precision alignment of the blade) is the ease of blade changing. The handles spring open to a detent, and pulling the handles farther apart past the detent, releases the blade for changing. Pull the old blade out, put the new one into position, and then carefully squeeze the handles together all the way. If you did it right (which is simple to do) the blade will self-align in its slot as the handles come fully together. After you do this a couple times, blade changes take maybe 10 seconds.

review_body:
I bought this vacuum to clean up after my attic renovation. I was excited to get this baby home and go to work cleaning up what was left from demolition. The first thing I noticed was that this vacuum has plenty of power. I sucked up just about anything and everything that had accumulated in the attic over the last 80 years. Nails, pieces of wood, matchbox cars, pieces of newspaper and little action figures. I think I only had the hose clog once or twice. The power cord is a good length, which is nice when using it as a vacuum or a blower. And the tool storage is great too, keeps everything close by when you need to change out attachments.

The filter it came with was good for cleaning up debris in the attic, and it's nice that they're washable. I used the blower to help dry the filter after washings. I got about 3-4 washings out of the filter before I tossed it. That filter does a good job for general purpose uses. During drywall, I switched to the top end filter and filter bags to catch all the drywall dust, it worked like a charm.

I use it as a blower almost as much as I use it as a vacuum. The blower is very strong and makes quick work of the yard. No complaints at all about the blower.

Pros:
- Very powerful, Long filter life, Can suck a lot between filter cleanings/changes, Maintains suction for quite a long time

Cons:
-The exhaust on the vacuum is strong too, it would blow stuff everywhere if it was pointed in a bad direction. They sell a muffler attachment for it though.

Overall I'm very happy with my purchase.

review_headline: The best and least expensive on Amazon
review_body:
These accessories for slat wall are the best available from Amazon and are the least expensive. What a combination!

I ordered a couple of hooks from each of the manufacturers to compare them. Jifram is the best in my view because of the included "stabilizers" and "double hook clips". The stabilizers are plastic inserts between the bottom of the hook and the slat wall. This locks the hooks in place horizontally and prevents the bottom from rotating up and allowing the hook from disconnect from the slat wall. The double hook clips allow you to connect two single hooks for a double. The double hook clips offer flexibility and are less expensive than buying a double hook. Neither the stabilizers or double hook clips are required. If you don't use them Jiframs hooks are like everyone else's. I appreciate and value the flexibility and have used them.

When compared to the competition, the hooks themselves seem the same. The distinction is the stabilizers and double hook clips. Making matters better, Jifram has the best prices.

review_body: Ordered this hole saw to cut a round opening in ceramic tile to fit over the shower drain. Worked perfectly. The tile was a mesh backed mosaic type and I was concerned that the saw would rip the small tiles off the netting while I was attempting to cut the hole through it. What I did to circumvent this problem is to take two pieces of 3/4" plywood slightly larger than the 12"x12" tile. I cut a 5" hole in the center of one of the pieces using a hole saw designed for wood, then I sandwiched the tile to be cut between the two pieces of wood so that the hole in the upper piece of wood with the hole cut in it was centered over the area of the tile to be cut out. I secured the two pieces of wood together by screws, thereby immobilizing the tile in between. With a spray bottle full of water at the ready, I began to cut the tile with this 4.5" diamond hole saw. This method allowed me to cut a perfect 4.5" hole exactly where I wanted it. There are probably other ways to accomplish such a task, but this method worked pretty well for me and was not overly time consuming. I would recommend this hole saw, especially considering that 4.5" hole saws available at the big box stores are MUCH closer to $100. This item, even with overnight shipping, came to only half of what I would have paid locally. No idea of the longevity of this item as it was ordered for a specific purpose and so have only had the opportunity to use it once. I would venture to guess that if used properly, keeping it WET during use, it should last several through several uses.

product_title: Bahco Alligator Adjustable Wrench
review_body:
This is the most intelligently engineered, sturdy, and useful adjustable wrench on the planet. I am a Marine Engineer and have been working with hands for the last 20 years and I can say that without reservation. It has never let me down, whether I had it on a 32mm nut with a cheater bar (see note below on modification), on a rounded off nut, or in hard to get to places.

The design is nearly perfect. That said, I did modified it slightly for my rig so that it works on 32mm nuts and bolts and the alligator end can accept larger pipes/nuts/bolts, etc.

If you're looking for an adjustable wrench, do yourself a favor and buy this... you'll be glad you did and will never need another.

product_title: LTM830160 - LEATHERMAN 830160 Surge Multi-Tool
review_body:
I've used the Surge since Oct 2011 and overall I think it's the best heavy-use multitool made. I used this tool at least twice a day just at work. I recently left it in a customer's bumper when using the great file that comes with it to clean terminals for a fog lamp (so sad). That file actually saved a backpacking trip in Kentucky when our water purification system was corroded due to the salt used for chlorine production. And I used that file to hone the knife.

There were two issues that keep it from being a 5-star item:

1. The scissors aren't great (as others have said not the best size) and the little plastic piece that gives extra purchase fell off almost instantly.

2. The wire cutter (mostly due to the design) cannot cut wire thicker than 16 gauge without binding and sometimes it bound up with thinner gauge.

Overall this tool rocks and I would recommended it to anyone in the automotive field. I like it so much that after I finish writing this review I am going to get another one right ...now.

product_title: Stanley STHT83166 2-Inch by 4-Inch Clamp
review_body:
I'm into woodworking and generally am not a fan of new tangled versions of standbys. Mostly I hate that plastic has replaced perfectly functional and useful tools. Clamps in particular take a beating but when the tool is metal, its not a big deal. When its plastic, it breaks.

The Stanley clamps are, mostly, plastic. They work like pipe clamps using the structural strength of the material. Pipe Clamps are , very adequate, work well and clamp securely though also very heavy. If you'd asked me if a 2x4 would have sufficed, I would have seriously doubted it.

I would have been wrong. These are excellent.

Using teeth that dig into the wood, the strength is impressive and the weight is not. All, this is an excellent way to clamp and I will be buying more for my shop!

product_title: Hot Shot Tactical HSSG12 MINI Beamlokr and Mini Tactical Light, Fits 12-Gauge, Black
review_body:
Really like this little rig.
PROs: It's light weight and light has three very useful modes - high beam, low bean, strobe with a zoom feature. It's all you need. The magnetic setup is compact and the Beamlokr unit attaches firmly to a 12 gauge barrel without any marring or scratching. I could see where recoil may move the light off its current position but by no means separate from the weapon when fired. I removed the attached cord from the tactical light as it was unnecessary in this configuration. The setup can be rotated of moved to different barrel position with ease. product_title: Craftsman 979918002 Table Saw Hand Wheel Assembly
review_headline: Be sure to measure your saw's shaft diameter!
review_body:
I have a 10\\" Craftsman contractor saw rescued from a yard sale a few years ago. Recently I had occasion to crank on the tilt hand wheel and found it was spinning on its hub. The plastic wheel molded around the \\"D\\" insert was old and had shattered.

I took a chance in ordering this hand wheel from Amazon without knowing the inside diameter of the hub. (This is the one critical dimension of the hand wheel and it's the one dimension not in the description.) Well, I lost. The shaft on my saw is an even 0.500\\" diameter. The ID of the hand wheel is 0.475\\". Since the hand wheel's insert is a \\"D\\", I can't bore it out. I just had to return it. So measure your saw's shaft diameter. If it's bigger than about 0.472\\", this wheel won't fit.

If it DOES fit your saw, you'll get one hollow-backed plastic hand wheel with a generous spinner knob. I would have been fine with it if it had worked with my saw. By the way, for some reason the product photo shows two wheels. You get one, not two.

Good luck.

product_title: SOG Specialty Knives & Tools Knife and Saw Tool
review_body: When a manufacturer releases a product like this, I find it down right insulting,  unless they are only charging a couple dollars....and I mean literally... 2 dollars.    Where to begin...    The steel is s***ty, but I won't beat the product up too much for that, as I knew this  would be the case.    The sheath is absolutely terrible.  Its actually the most insulting part about the product.  You see.....the knife doesn't fit into it!  IT DOESN'T FIT!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!  I normally don't beat knives up too much because of low quality sheaths they may come with,  but this is a specialty item with a revolving saw, and it would really help if the manufacturer  could at the very least give us a functional sheath, so we can carry it with us.  You are going to  have to make your own sheath for it if you ever want to carry it with you, and because of the weird design, that may be difficult for you.    The blade....its like a thinned out cheaper version of their seal knife.  Of course there are serrations,  SOG puts serrations on everything.  I don't get it....I mean the saw integrated design indicates that  the idea behind this is wilderness use....how many of us using our knives out there in the bush  want serrations on our knives?  Almost none....SOG is clueless.    The handle...is a very hard unforgiving material with finger groves! Great!  So not only is the material  uncomfortable....but you've designed finger grooves that only allow me to hold the knife one way.  Thanks  SOG!  Between the finger grooves and the serrations on the blade....you end up with a knife that is completely unusable in the wilderness.    The saw....it actually works fine.  However.....it really needs to be about an inch longer.  At the length  it is, you really can't saw anything with it that you couldn't tackle with your multi-tool saw.  I always carry a multi-tool that has a saw blade in my pocket when I'm out in the bush.  Because of that, I just have  no use for this at all.Further negativity....  This thing is downright dangerous.  I don't trust the locking system at all.  The knife and saw are one  long solid piece that revolves.  The end you aren't using pushes into the handle.  Weak looking pins keep the knife or saw from continuing to swing around and cutting into your hand.  The blades and locking  mechanism rattle terribly, giving me absolutely no confidence in its strength.  I honestly feel its dangerous, and wouldn't even use it in my yard at home, nor would I sell or trade it to a friend.    So what do you end up with?    A poorly designed knife made from poor steel that is not very useful as a knife in the bush, with an  uncomfortable and unsafe handle.  You will have a functional saw.....but you would be better served  carrying a multitool with a saw blade.....at least that you could keep in your pocket....because as I mentioned above...the sheath accompanying this thing doesn't fit, so you have no way of carrying it with you.    I think they could have made this decent without too much work.  Clean up the action on the locking mechanism  so it doesn't rattle so much and we might have a little more confidence in it.  take off the serrations on the blade, and the grooves on the handle.  Oh yeah......and lengthen the freakin sheath a little bit ya donkey......its just insulting!

product_title: PowerSmith MLSTR12 Mag lithium 12-Volt Lithium Ion Starter Kit with Charger and Battery Pack
review_body:
This is a replacement charger for one I received as part of a Combo Kit in 2010. I made the mistake of leaving the old one outside in a terrific rainstorm and it (quite understandably) died. I have two batteries from the Combo Kit ([[ASIN:B004T1W1AS PowerSmith PL205PCK2 20v Lithium-Ion 5 Piece Combo Kit, Green]])and decided to go ahead and purchase this one with another battery as I often have two tools up and running on the same project(frequently the hand saw and the drill). For $10 more, I added another battery so I can have two tools ready and a battery in the charger.

Upon receiving the charger, I pulled out my two (by that time) very dead batteries and started charging them. I then made sure the new battery I received was also at full charge. The unit smelled a little \\"hot electric plastic\\" for the first several hours but not in a dangerous way, I've had a few things actually catch on fire and believe me, I know the difference. By the time I charged the last battery and put everything away in the bag that came with the Combo Kit, the smell was gone.

My experience with PowerSmith products has been wonderful. I am rough on tools and tend to push them to their limits. These have survived more than three years with me and have been used in the extremely hot, dry environment of the Mojave desert usually being stored in the back of a truck where temperatures can easily reach well over 110 f. The batteries store well, holding a charge in either hot or cold weather. The charger, which is admittedly a little finicky about starting to charge, once the battery is seated well, does a very nice, quick job. I am sold on lithium powered hand tools and I am sold on PowerSmith quality.

product_title: Fluidmaster 550DFRK Duo Flush Complete System
review_body:
I bought three of these from a local big box store and installed them in the three different toilet models in my home. After two weeks, I'm satisfied with how they work, but not wowed. I'll have to wait a few months to see if they do anything for my water bill.

Some observations:
- Installation was very easy. The first one took a half hour or so including reading instructions, removing the old toilet guts, and figuring out which (if any) adapters I needed. The third one took 10 minutes including removal of old parts. I'm only moderately handy.

- The flush handle is a bit awkward on a toilet that was not designed for upward handle movement. All three models required me to angle the handle down slightly to allow room to lift up for the half flush. This is a cosmetic issue, but could be significant if you are particular about such things.

- There is a learning curve with how to flush. There is a sweet spot with holding the handle for just a split second before releasing in order to get a flush each time. My littlest child, 6, is not having the easiest time with the half-flush while my 10 year old seemed to pick it up pretty quickly. Even after a couple of weeks of practice, I still miss the mark occasionally and only get a partial half flush that doesn't do the trick.

- There is a distinct variance in function with each individual toilet. It works best in my large tank Kohler, well in my Bemis, and is functional but more finicky in my Universal/Rundle. The flush settings also followed the same pattern from lowest setting to highest.

- I have not found any leakage or issues with the water continuing to run as is documented by other reviewers here.

Bottom line: I would recommend.

Well, here I am three months later. My observations:

- My last water/sewer bill (quarterly) was higher than the one before I installed these.
- The most used toilet has begun to leak a bit and I hear it squirting a splash of water into the tank off and on even though no one has used it recently.
- I think the inconsistent flush issue has worsened rather than improved with practice. I notice that the toilet in my kids' bathroom is often un-flushed while I find it increasingly more difficult to find the \\"sweet spot\\" I mentioned in my first review.

review_headline: Bosch is THE KING of GRINDERS
review_body:
I have been using angle grinders for work in one manner or another for 20 years. After trying most every brand and style, I can confidently say that Bosch is the KING of them. DeWalt may own the cordless drill title, but they cant touch Bosch in the grinder market.

There are various sizes, with this among the smaller grip and body size. This is slightly larger than the average 4.5\\" grinder body, but not so much as to be uncomfortable. This grinder is noticably smaller and lighter than the 7\\" to 10\\" grinder variations.

The main issue of concern with this and all 6\\" grinders is that they are primarily made as cut off grinders, meaning there are very few grinding blades available. They are out there, but often they are only available from industrial supply companies. HomeDepot or Lowes usually do not carry anything besides cut off wheels in the 6\\" range. Grinding, wire, and other types of blade/wheels, are readily available in the 4.5\\" and 7\\" to 10\\" sizes, but not as much for the 6\\".

If this is the right size for you, and you are not hampered by the lack of wheels other than the cut-off types, this is the grinder you want. The Bosch grinders are on the higher end of the price range, but they are well worth it related to quality and durability.

These levels are definitely basic. No one will mistake them for expensive tools. They're just basic levels in basic, red plastic. However they appear solid and for how I will use them, I expect them to last years.

I hesitated for a long time about buying them, but I'm glad I finally overcame my skepticism.

review_body:
These belts are as described. Good value for a batch of 10 assorted. Note that there're open coat*. (Open or closed coat doesn't matter to me on these belts as I use this sander for fast sanding wood (not finish sanding), chamfering bolts that have been cut shorter, sanding plastic, etc.) Two of the belts sent to me had some fraying on the edges that was easily trimmed with scissors - ran the belts and it didn't get worse. Hence the 4 stars instead of 5. Came with a 10% off coupon for your next Peachtree order with Amazon.

*Open coat means 50%-70% of the backing material is coated with the abrasive so it doesn't load up as fast as closed coat. Closed coat means 100% of the backing is coated with the abrasive, hence it's longer lasting and more aggressive since there's more abrasive per unit of area. Open coat is recommended for \\"gummy\\" materials that could load a belt or disc such as soft woods, aluminum, plastic, etc. Closed coat is recommended for hard woods and finish sanding.

review_body:

The Leakfrog's battery compartment screws stripped out very easily, so I replaced them with these. These are louder than the Leakfrogs, which will help (I didn't hear our Leakfrog go off until I passed by the door to the basement).
Be sure to read the instructions about how to open them, and how to install the battery: battery placement is important, apparently, in keeping the device upright and floating.
I installed one of these in my mom's crawl space, by her sump pump, and I tethered it to the crawlspace ceiling with a thumbtack (into the ceiling) and fishing line (tied to the thumbtack and taped to the leak detector, with a few inches of slack) so the device wouldn't end up in the bottom of the sump, in case the power goes out, crawlspace floods, power comes back on, pump empties water, and the floating leak detector ends up in a bad place.
These supposedly emit a signal when the battery runs low, but I'll test them every half year anyway: wet finger, touch the contacts, listen for the SOS beep (dit-dit-dit, dot... dot... dot... dit-dit-dit), and dry off the contacts.

product_title: Triton TRA001 3-1/4 HP Dual Mode Precision Plunge Router
review_headline: So far so good...Router Table use only
review_body:
Bought this over the past month and have used it on an entertainment center cutting dados, templates, edge profiles all in a router table. My previous router experiences include three craftsman routers (last two were horrible) and then a dewalt router (wonderful router). Here are some thoughts:

Weight: This thing is top heavy and is primarily meant for table use. You will have difficulty unless using it on a larger flat surface or with more complex jigs, even when using the edge guide.

Power: Cuts through any hardwood, plywood, and melamine with no problem using sharp bits. Like the slow start and adjustable speed. Overall scare factor is low to moderate (healthy respect for it) but not high.

Functioning: This is where I find it to shine. It seemed a bit gimmicky at first, but once I got used to it, I realized it is a well thought out piece of equipment with bells and whistles that make sense and are actually useful. Ofcourse, some of them are not as useful mounted in my table. I really like the bit changing features where you can truly do it with one handle and don't have to jam your fist into something trying to loosen it.

Table Mount: I used the Kreg PRS3034 Insert Plate, which is made to go with this router and works well. The above table adjustability is like having a lift. I will be adding an offset wrench for convenience of bit changing. So far, cuts have been right on. On my dewalt I would get a little movement after making an adjustment and then clamping down the router into the base. Since there is no base, there is no movement after making an adjustment.

Dust collection: I used it for a few above table plunge cuts and fount dust collection to be really great compared to my dewalt when hooked up to a vacuum. It picked up 90% of dust using shop vac. The plastic around the base and the built in vacuum opening fits my Shop-vac Universal Tool Adapter. In the table, dust collection is great, but I believe that is more the table than the router.

Reliability: Cannot speak to this yet. I at least feel good in how there is protection built into the switch and other areas to reduce dust getting into it. Read other reviews on recommendations/cautions. I do remove the spring in table mounting it.

Expections: I am a hobbiest and use this on a monthly basis versus a daily/weekly basis. I made a router table top and use this with the Kreg plate and levelers and have a very accurate system with clean cuts. I would buy this again for the stated purpose of a table router only. I do not plan on using this for above table use because it is just too big and top heavy. I mostly make sawdust and then occassionally build furniture.

Update: July 2014 After numerous projects including cabinetry using stile and rail bit system, I have found the durability to be solid. In fact, I never mess with this thing other than changing bits. I leave it in my router table and use it solely for that purpose. The above table lift feature still works. Still very pleased with this router.

product_title: Streamlight 88030 ProTac 1L 275 Lumen Professional Tactical Flashlight with High/Low/Strobe w/ 1 x CR123A Batteries
review_headline: Very Nice Tactical Light With a Couple Gotchas
review_body:
This is a very well made tac light, very bright and compact. It uses a lithium battery which means it can sit around for years and still be ready when you need it. I like it, but there are a couple things to be aware of, especially for a tactical light, which means something that has to be 100% reliable and ready when you need it.

1) Hitting the mode you want is very tricky. You have to hit the switch just the right number of times (of course) and most tricky at just the right interval. The timing is VERY fast and it is different if you are going to use a particular mode temporarily (light press and hold button) or switching to that mode (press firmly and release staying on that mode). It takes practice, lots of it to hit the mode you want reliably.

2) When the battery runs out, there is absolutely NO WARNING. Either you will click it on and nothing happens or (most of the time) you will click it on and in a few seconds it goes dead. NOT a good situation for a tactical light. The only way this light can be absolutely ready for a critical situation is to put a new fresh $4 battery in it. Battery life isn't great, but that's the price for such a bright light running on a single CR123 battery. Just hope it is ready when you need it. A low battery indicator would be nice.

Still I gave it a soft 4 stars, maybe 3.5 would be more precise. It is a good light if you use it often enough to be good at hitting the right mode and if you have a fresh battery in it.

product_title: BLACK+DECKER BDCS80I 8V MAX Impact Screwdriver
review_body:
I've had the opportunity to spend a few weeks with this impact driver prior to its release, courtesy of Black & Decker.

First impressions:
The product is packaged well in an attractive box. The box was smaller than I had anticipated and upon opening it, I was surprised at how compact the driver is. It's definitely not your standard drill/driver. The manual is well-written and informative. That's increasingly hard to find, so I appreciated that small point. I put the driver on the charger (B&D recommends a nine-hour initial charge) and let it charge overnight. The charger has a special plug on it and I've never been a fan of proprietary plugs and ports, but I can't say it's really ever been an issue for me. There is a nice charge indicator light on the bottom of the driver that blinks when charging and remains solid once the battery is full.

The BDCS801 features a 1/4\\" quick-release hex chuck, but it is not magnetic, so you will want an adapter for straight-shafted bits. There is, however, a magnetic holder for the driver bit, which I found extremely useful compared to the standard snap-in holders I'm used to that require you to force the bit into a tight slot (I always have a hard time getting bits in and out of those). After using the magnetic holder, I would like to see a couple more provided because I am often switching back and forth between a few different bits. To install a bit, just pull the collar forward, insert the bit, and release the collar. There is also an LED light ahead of the trigger that you can turn on without activating the driver. I used the light just last night in the dark of my garage and it helped me place the bit on the screw head; no complaints there. At just under 1.5 pounds, the driver is hefty enough to lend a solid, quality feel without causing fatigue after long use. You could throw it in your back pocket if you choose.

Usage notes:
My first project was to drive screws and bolts into a cornhole (bags) game set I'm building. Speed and force control through the trigger is smooth and linear, which is great because of how much power you're working with. With light jobs, you are able to drive in the screw without activating the impact mechanism. It's only after the driver encounters more resistance that the impact mechanism is activated, creating more torque. The impact hammer certainly makes it loud compared to standard drivers, but it is quieter than other impacts I have seen (especially air guns). The driver has plenty of power to counter-sink your screws without having to drill counter-sink holes. In fact, just for fun, I took a screw to a pine 2x4 and was able to drive the head halfway through the wood without any pre-drilling. This little guy is very powerful. With the linearity of the trigger, you are able to set your screw depth right where you want it. I also used a 3/8\\" socket adapter and a socket to remove the lug nuts on my car (AFTER having already loosened them); it speeds the process up quite nicely. (Note: Ensure you use a proper torque wrench to re-install your lug nuts.)

A little more on the force control with the trigger: I really like being able to use the trigger to fine-tune the amount of force I want to apply. With my other driver, I typically pick a torque figure on the clutch ring, attempt to drive the screw, find out I'm under powered, stop driving, bump up the torque, try again, and repeat until I've got the screw sunk to just where I want it. This process is much faster and easier with the B&D and you never have to stop and adjust.

B&D claims the battery will hold its charge for 18 months. My 19.2 volt Craftsman ni-cad batteries require charging if they have sat unused for more than a couple weeks. That is a substantial benefit of a lithium-ion battery over the old nickel-cadmium batteries. You could easily drive 150 screws with this driver before you need to recharge. However,the battery is not removable or replaceable, so you won't be able to swap in a fresh battery if you're planning a particularly heavy use day. That being said, the battery life I've experienced is nothing short of phenomenal. But heck, at this price point, you could always buy two; maybe throw one in your car.

Summary:
The Black & Decker BDCS801 Impact Driver is a highly versatile, very portable tool at a great price. In my opinion, this driver would be a deal at anything under a hundred bucks. I've been very pleased and the BDCS801 has become my go-to tool for jobs around the house. The only reason I keep my older drill/driver around is for drilling, since I don't yet have any hex-headed drill bits. I highly recommend this driver without hesitation and look forward to completing a lot of projects with it. This is the best cordless impact driver I've used.the battery is not removable or replaceable, so you won't be able to swap in a fresh battery if you're planning a particularly heavy use day. That being said, the battery life I've experienced is nothing short of phenomenal. But heck, at this price point, you could always buy two; maybe throw one in your car.

product_title: Pocket Chain Saw
review_headline: Sharp, Well Made, Light Weight and Convenient
review_body:
I just used this Handy Pocket chain saw to cut 6 "branches" that were shooting up out out of the ground around a large tree in my yard. The limbs were between 1/2" and 2" in diameter, and the saw cut through them with little difficulty. Although the cuts were not quite as clean as a gas-powered chain saw (mostly because I cut them myself, without a buddy to take the other end), they were satisfactory.

The chain bites well, and can be used at just about any angle - wrapped around a limb with your right hand in one strap and your left in the other, or held straight out between 2 people and articulated back and forth. It will adapt to just about any size of limb or branch.

It comes with a handy belt pouch, so you can keep the sharp edges out of your way while doing other chores, and pull it right out when you need it. It sure beats carrying a heavy chainsaw with you for small jobs, and you don't have to fight with it to get it to start!

The chain itself looks and feels very much like a typical chain saw blade, and the hardware connecting it to the soft straps is sturdy (probably made of steel). It's very heavy-duty, and looks like it will last a good long time.

I'd recommend it for hikers, mountain bikers, campers - anyone who spends a little time in the woods. Also, it would be a great tool to keep in your emergency kit.

5 starts for a great product!
