review_body:
We had an older pair of these before they went to the glossy black casing, and have used those for the better part of the last decade or more, and they worked amazing. The reason for getting new ones is heck- after over a decade and just starting to have the surround padding for the ears get a little hard and torn, they are a steal of a deal for the price you pay to protect your hearing.

The work we do:
Table Saws, Band Saws, Power Sanders, Planers, Leaf Blowers, Chainsaws, Rifle and Shotgun Shooting (more fun, less work...), Lawn Mowers, Jack Hammers. Basically anything construction- these have been used for- even the occasional night when my dad with poor hearing cranks up the tv to hurting volumes to my sensitive hearing- I have nothing to say but good things.

They work amazing at deadening outside sound, and for me- I can still hear people talking but the really noise-damaging sounds are drastically cut down. If you want to listen to music with these, I highly recommend a pair of sound-isolating ear buds, and NOT the iPhone/iPod standard ones. When I do this- my volume is nearly kept at the minimum volume for most tasks, and sometimes even that was too loud- so the good news being, you can hear music with a GOOD set of speakers, keep the volume low to avoid hearing loss, and at the same time- get the comfort and added protection from outside sounds with these. The in-ear work better than around the ear, however.

I have also used these with (and they recommend) thin-sided glasses, safety or otherwise (I use some Oakley Antix) and (especially on the new pair with newer padding around the ears) they still cut out exterior sound to a really good degree, nearly the same as without the exterior interference. Highly recommended so long as you don't mind keeping a hat off. If you want one- get an oversize hat or a cheapie you don't mind getting bent a little out of shape from the over-head hearing as the wires stick out about a quarter to half-inch from your skin.

Also- I have a HUGE head (translation: I wear extra large hats and not all one-size fits all hats fit me.. I think I was 7.25-7.5 on a fitted cap when I played little league baseball...) and very large ears (maybe 3\\" top to bottom..? they run in the family, oh well..) but these still have expansion space to fit on even larger heads and my ears fit inside the cups PERFECTLY. Unless you are part of the 1% of the population with a freakishly large (no offense) head or ears, they should work perfectly for you, so hopefully that answers that question if you're wondering how they work for larger heads.

The only disadvantage I see is with shooting sports, particularly rifle and shotgun. They stick out enough to the point that if you sight down the barrel- they interfere and get pushed out of the way by the rifle/shotgun stock. Would def. recommend a slim set. I went with some Howard Leight ones that work pretty well on battery-operated silencing, however they are not so great if you sweat. These are basically waterproof and don't get sticky like my Howard Leight ones when dry and are easy to maintain. Both are really great quality but bang for the buck... these can not be beat. product_title: Bosch 4100 10-Inch Worksite Table Saw
review_body:
Approaching retirement, I thought I would treat myself to this, as I have wanted a table saw since my teens, and have made do with totally inadequate substitutes. This has raised my game considerably. I can now cut accurate and repeatable cuts. I explored cheaper saws and rejected them. One of those had a reputation for its settings wandering (that's the main reason I chucked my first inexpensive router away - what's the point of a tool where the depth you cut changes from the start to the finish?) Another would not take a dado blade, and so forth. The Bosch was the least expensive that seemed as if it would do everything I needed, and do it properly, and so it has proved.

The first time I did a cross cut, I was amazed at how clean and smooth the cut was. Ripping too produces clean surfaces. I thought I would need to buy a blade with a higher tooth count for smooth crosscuts (the supplied blad is only 40 teeth), but the one that came with the saw cuts both well and both cross and rip with ease. The first thing I built was a cabinet for it to stand on. The frames went together perfectly. Exactly square and no wind or racking. Built a finger joint jig, fitted the dado blade and made the drawers. Again, perfect.

I am very, very pleased with this.

I would advise, as I did, buying the side and rear extensions. They are not expensive and do give a support for wider and longer workpieces. Also, buy (or make) a couple of feather boards.

The only thing I've been disappointed with was the separately purchased dado zero clearance insert. Didn't like it, so I made my own out of 3/8 ply.

product_title: SE 82331TF 30-Piece Set of Titanium-Coated Diamond Burrs
review_body:
Tiny dynamos, this set of diamond burs really works, and so far as I can tell, really is diamond. I didn't expect anything else, but I had to test it to be sure. I wanted such a set for occasional fine work on very hard items like tool steel and rock.

Pros
* Perfect fit (diameter = 0.122 in.) for my Dremel multitool
* These burs will grind anything -- masonry nails, titanium nitride coating on drill bits, tungsten carbide bit tips, you name it
* They do not self-destruct on usage
* The set contains a huge variety of shapes (spindles, barrels, balls, needle tips, concave and convex angles, etc.)
* The set is safe in a surprisingly nice case insert -- I like that it's a soft foam, cut to securely hold the bits

Cons
* None discovered

Other thoughts
The product photo shows these looking more like titanium nitride-coated bits, but they're actually silvery in appearance, and given that they are able etch and cut the hardest, most durable things in my tool collection, I'm inclined to believe they're the real deal, but at an exceptionally affordable price.

product_title: wolfcraft 3751405 Dowel Pro Doweling Kit
review_body:
I gave this doweling jig three stars, what I'd call average; because that's the best result I can get from it.
For reference I almost always use dowels for edge joins. I have a different jig I use for edge to face joins.
On the plus side it allows me to drill the two mating holes on the same setup and in that respect the holes line up well.
Out of the box the quality is adequate but appears to be another fairly cheap Chinese tool. Its main problem is accuracy; it's always about 1/64th or 1/32nd off on the join. Also, the 3/8\\", 5/16\\", and ¼\\" holes are not on the same center line on the jig so it places the ¼\\" and 5/16\\" holes very close to the edge of the piece so the thicker the stock, the larger the unsupported area you'll have. The jig is definitely biased towards ½\\" or 5/8\\" thick stock regarding edge joins.
This jig is probably OK for basic utility joints but in my opinion it's not for situations where you need accurate joins that don't require lots of cleanup afterwards. The jig is a decent concept but is hindered by mediocre build quality.
Other reviewers have claimed to get very accurate joins. I don't doubt their claim and perhaps I have a defective unit, but that is also another potential concern for others.

product_title: Dremel 7300-PT 4.8-Volt Pet Grooming Kit
review_headline: Easier on dogs, but the battery is pretty dreadful
review_body:
We used this Dremel for about 1.5 years, and we have 2 shelties and we do their nails once a week. After just a few months of using this, the battery wouldn't charge much at all (even though we'd completely drain it before charging it) so it wouldn't be as fast, and we'd be able to do 2 paws before the battery crapped out entirely. Still, we put up with it and nursed it along, and made it work for us (doing 2 paws a day, 4 days a week) until the 1 year mark when it really got bad and unusable. So I bought a replacement battery and THAT battery had the same problem. We nursed it along for 6 months until we said to heck with it.

So for the Dremel 7300-PT, the battery was a big issue, the product didn't work as well as it could have because of it. We bought this Dremel 7300-PT in mid-2011, and bought the replacement battery in mid-2012. Unless they've done a sweeping overhaul of the battery, I would stay away from this specific model as well as the Dremel Mini-Mite which uses the same battery.

I liked the Dremel concept though - grinding their nails versus clipping seemed to be preferable to our dogs. They still weren't super thrilled about nail grooming, but nothing a treat afterwards can't fix, right? =) After giving up on this pet Dremel, we replaced it with another Dremel: [[ASIN:B003TU0XEQ Dremel 7000-N/5 6-Volt Cordless Two-Speed Rotary Tool]]. I'm able to put Eneloop rechargeable batteries in it and they last a long time. It's higher powered, and with coarse grit sander bands the whole nail grooming process is done and over with much sooner, which the pups appreciate.

Note: I think you should do yourself and your dog a favor and get coarse grit 1/2\\" sander bands to use (fine grit bands are included with this Dremel 7300-PT). The grinding goes much faster with the coarse grit and our dogs were even less fussy about nail grooming time when we switched to coarse grit. These are the bands I use: [[ASIN:B00004UDGW Dremel 408 1/2-Inch Sander Bands, Coarse, 6 Pack]]408 1/2-Inch Sander Bands, Coarse, 6 Pack]]

product_title: LED Lenser - V DUAL COLOR
review_body:
I have a strange obsession with flashlights. I volunteer as a camp counselor during the summers and having a good, durable, quality light is invaluable. A bright white light is necessary for keeping track of campers at night, and a red light is necessary for being able to see at night in a cabin without disturbing others.

Normally I buy 90% of my camping gear from Amazon, but in this case I found these lights for DIRT cheap on a popular clearance website and bought three of them. The upside here is I have a good feel for the quality of these lights after opening and using three of them.

Pros:
The white light is very bright.
The red light is fairly bright. (You don't want this to be blinding as it would defeat the purpose of a red light...)
The light is small and easy to carry in a pocket without feeling obtrusive.
Water resistant so I don't have to fear rain / broken hydration bladders / drooling campers.
The case, lanyard, and carabiner they come with are a really awesome touch. I wish more flashlights had that.

Cons:
-1/3 of the lights I opened had a pretty "broken" feeling white light button which I fully expect will eventually fail me.
-The buttons don't feel very sturdy in general. Really loose and insubstantial.
-The textured/smooth button design idea was a great IDEA but very poorly executed. If you can feel the difference between the buttons you have much more sensitive fingers than I do. I have to scrape the buttons with my fingernail to figure out if it's textured. But even then it'd be easier to just click the button and find out by trial and error.

Summary:
Overall this is a great light. Certainly overpriced if you bought it at it's original $30. At the Amazon $22 I don't think you'll be disappointed. The cons regarding the "feeling" of the buttons are just about the feeling that they will break. They haven't, and still work fine, so I may just be paranoid.

I don't believe you'll be disappointed with this purchase.

product_title: PORTER-CABLE 20-Volt 1/2-Inch Lithium-Ion Drill/Driver Kit
review_body:
Wow! The Porter-Cable PCCK600LB 20-volt 1/2-Inch Lithium Ion Drill/Driver is a lot of tool. This drill is beefy well built and can take on any job that a person might face. I really like it.

Here are some things that you might want to know about the drill--in my opinion:

The battery and accompanying charger work well and the condition of the battery can be monitored a couple of ways. You can't over charge the battery and the spare can be left in the charger until needed. The compact Lithium battery snaps easily onto the tool and comes back off without any trouble at all.

The Lithium battery is smaller and not as heavy as the battery pack found on most drills using a high voltage power source.

The onboard battery gauge is very useful and somewhat unique to this Porter Cable 20 V drill. A quick press of a button shows how much juice is left in the battery. The charger also has a built-in gauge capable of analyzing the battery health as well as displaying the charging progress. By the way, the 20 V batteries charge up quickly in usually less than an hour.

The power is excellent. I have used my Porter Cable PCCK600LB 20-Volt drill to remove and drive three inch deck screws with no problem. I also put a three quarter inch hole through an oak board with a spade bit and the tool did that easily. I chucked a six inch buffing wheel into the drill and cleaned up some dirty hardware with no problem.

The drilling capacity of this tool is outstanding.

It can handle putting holes in almost any material and the chuck holds a bit steady with no discernible wobble. The keyless chuck is the best one I have seen on a cordless drill. It is well designed, smooth to operate and tightens around a bit as well as a keyed chuck does.

The 22 clutch variations and a two position torque switch provide enough in the way of adjustment for any job I can think of.

The trigger switch provides speed control of course. The forward/reverse button is located where it should be and similar to what one would find on other drills.

I appreciate the built-in LED work light. That feature is becoming standard on most drill brands and the one on the Porter-Cable is typical, but not outstanding. In fact, the light beam does not quite illuminate a screw head or the mark for drilling a hole because the chuck is in the way causing a shadow in the wrong place. This is especially true with a short bit in the chuck. The light helps in a general way, but it is located in a bad spot on the drill for optimum illumination of a bit or drill point. It is better than guessing in the dark or holding a flashlight in your teeth.

The magnetic drill bit holders are a good idea--better than spring clips or plastic slots found on most drills.

The tough plastic storage box is easy to haul around, but there is no room in there for much else other than the tool, a spare battery and the charger. Screw driver bits and assorted drills will have to travel in your pocket.

The drill/driver looks pretty good to me, but I am not sure how the appearance might impress a professional builder out on the job. I read a review of this tool that said it looked like it was made out of Legos. That is probably an exaggeration. However, the tool does have a plastic feel about it and it is a bit gaudy. That has nothing to do with how tough it is. This is a sturdy piece of equipment.

The PCCK600LB drill is well made with the fit and finish just about perfect. There is a lot of excellence built into this tool. One thing that most people might not notice is the presence of substantial rubber bumpers on each side and rear of the tool so setting it down on a rough or wet surface won't scratch it up or get dirt into the cooling slots. Good thinking Porter Cable.

The belt clip is really not practical. The drill, although lighter than most, is still pretty heavy (3.5 lbs.) and it pulls my pants down when hooked to my belt. The belt clip that comes separately with the drill kit does not need to be installed. After attaching the clip and trying it out briefly I removed the clip in order keep my pants up.

The drill will set upright on a flat surface with the battery as a base. I guess all cordless drills do that.

I find the drill to be somewhat long and that limits its use to more open sites. That is no doubt where it belongs anyhow. This tool is even somewhat shorter than similar cordless drills, but it is still hard to get into tight spots.

This is the tool you would use for building a deck, hanging a door, building a fence or putting holes in two-by-fours. Even so, the drill can handle a lot of DIY applications around the house.

There is a good one year parts and service warranty provided with this tool which includes a 90 day money back guarantee.

I chose the Stanley because the high visibility yellow fits in with other Stanley and Dewalt tools I plan to buy. product_title: Black and Decker PS160 12 Volt Battery Charger #418352-01
review_body:
I purchased one of these seveal years ago and it cooked the first time I used it. Checked the battery (B&D PS130) afterwards and it was dead, 0V across the terminals. When out and bought a new battery for that project. Afterwards discharged the battery (proper way to store Ni-Cd batteries) and stored it for next project. When that came, spent another $15 on a new charger, and same thing, fried.

Not quite willing to give up since it's for a three-piece kit and it's the only jig saw I still have and rarely use, did some investigation for my most recent project. First, this battery charger electronics is nothing more than a poorly designed rectifier and current limiter...and if too much current is pulled through it the resistor cooks until it fries the board or opens. Second, researched and found that the Dewalt DW9116 charges these batteries (again, PS130). So instead of wasting another $15 on this, bought the DW9116 (~$30), and it brought both batteries back to life and with quite a good bit of charge capacity (one is ~8 years old, the other ~3 years).

Even if you're trying to pinch pennies, and I'm good at going cheap, this is a useless item. Instead, please donate the money to the Red Cross or a twelve pack of good brew.

product_title: DELTA 34-184 Universal-Deluxe Tenoning Jig
review_body:
I purchased this jig because Wood Magazine rated it tops and it was on sale at Amazon. It arrived as promised, well packed and in good shape. This thing is a tank, it weights a ton and the workmanship is better than what I have come to expect from the typical made in China product. I cleaned everything, using WD40 and assembled it in about 20 minutes. I did not need the washers that are supplied on the miter bar for use with saws that have T-slots. I removed them. The first thing I found was that it will not fit the older, or for all I know, the newer, Craftsman table saws. The older saws had a miter slot that was about .007 inch less than the standard .750 inch slot. I removed the miter bar and with about 10 minutes work on a belt sander had it fitting perfectly. Once in the miter slot the base had no wobble and sat rock solid on the table. The issue noted with the miter bar adjustment screws did not concern me.

This jig is designed to be used on the left side of the blade and I prefer to cut with it on the right side. As shipped the base will hit the blade. There is a second set of holes for the miter bar that will move it out. However, the thickness of the stock will be limited. I wish that they had added a third set of miter bar mounting holes to allow for thicker stock. Another problem using the jig on the right side is that the face plate is very close to the base. When the stock has to be clamped above the base plate you can not set the blade height by referencing the table, you must reference from a spacer that is thicker than the base. I can't hold this against Delta as they planned for it for use on the left side. But a bit more thought by the designer could have eliminated this problem.

Squaring the jig to the blade was not a big problem. Adjusting the thickness of the cut should be simple, just loosen the clamp, set the depth, tighten the clamp and you should be good to go. The problem is that if the clamp is loose enough to slide the base the face plate will tilt, slightly. This makes a precise setting difficult. This is the main reason that I only give it three stars.

product_title: Streamlight MicroStream Ultra-compact Aluminum body with AAA Alkaline Battery
review_headline: Awesome tiny light with more than 3.5 battery life
review_body:
This is my latest favorite among my rather large flashlight collection. Reasons:

- It is tiny as AAA lights tend to be. Very light and pocketable.
- Great pocket clip. Can be used top down or top up. Can be clipped onto a baseball hat as a headlamp. No sharp edges to tear up the pockets.
- Easy one setting, a relatively bright 28 lumens. No need to fuss with multiple modes. I have reasons to think it is actually a bit brighter than they advertise.
- Good bright hotspot with plenty of spill on the side. Really good use of the small LED emitter. The hotspot is bright enough to illuminate things even during the day.
- Best clicky switch I have seen lately. Very easy to activate momentary on with minimal pressure, but needing a strong push to actually click for permanent on. Momentary-on clickies have become my favorite because they allow plenty of versatility (you can even spell out Morse code if you wanted to). However, most momentary clickies require some amount of pressure to activate and feel mushier than this one; some of the worst activate right before they also click on for permanent on; this is the opposite. I can't overemphasize how nice the switch is.
- Runtime, as I measured it with Sanyo Eneloop AAA, was 3 hrs and 40 minutes, more than an hour longer than advertised, or almost 50% more than advertised!

Overall, I am stunned by the low price and beyond-spec performance of this little wonder. You get a flashlight which is brighter and lasts longer than advertised, and has a super simple user interface. It would make a great gift as well due to its price and ease of use (in fact, I got it as a gift).

Highly recommended!

product_title: Neiko 10207A 3" Mini Bench Grinder and Polisher with Flexible Shaft and Accessories | 120W | 0-10000 RPM
review_body:
I am a wood turner who specializes in hollow forms. I make my own hollowing tools. My main grinder is an 8\\" (slow, 1725 rpm) with 80 grit Norton SX (K hardness) on both ends - the 100/120 grit wheels are J hardness, and don't balance as well with a precision dresser, so I can't use them.

I make my cutters from square stock of HSS/10% Co. To shape them I bevel the edges of the stone and work them from the side of the stone to the front. I was doing fine with my 8\\" with 3/16 and 1/4\\" cutters - but it was difficult to work with 1/8\\" cutters. I decided to give the 3\\" grinder a try. One night of working with it and I'm sold.

This is why I'm sold on it for my purposes. The wheel is quite soft and cuts slowly, that works on my small cutters as I have to shape them free hand and don't want to take too much off. I can get down in close to it so I can see the angle I'm grinding (which varies as I go from tip to sides of the cutters. I have control of my grinding. It is good for sensitive work.

I did have to modify it for my usage - there wasn't enough room between the inside of the wheel and the inside frame for me to use the left side of the wheel. I shimmed the wheel outward along the shaft by about a half inch with fender washers. There was still enough shaft to keep the wheel steady. It cost me the use of the flex shaft, but I didn't need that in the first place.

Let me comment on some of the complaints in the other reviews. The packaging of grinding wheel and fiber wheel as pairs: you can get the individual wheels online from MicroMark.com for $9.20 for either. They sell this machine with a different label (and a lot more money - $70). The grinding wheel they sell is 120 grit, and the one that came with this Neiko seems to be about that, and both are a 10mm arbor hole.

The speed control is a bit jinky when you crank it up, that is because this is a very low horsepower machine. Put it up to high speed then back off once the wheel is turning, that reduces the starting load.

And that raises a question of speed equivalence. I was a bit disturbed at first when I found the motor slowing when grinding at the low speeds I wanted, there isn't enough power to grind HSS at low speed - then I realized that the speed of grinding isn't the RPM, it is the inches per second (or feet per minute). A 3\\" wheel running at 4500 RPM is the equivalent of an 8\\" wheel running at 1725 RPM at the contact surface - the greater the diameter of the wheel the faster (in linear measure) the grinding. I raised the RPM and it worked fine.

The tool rest is tiny, and not very strong - but this machine is designed more for free hand grinding than high pressure. I used only one screw to bolt it on so I can use it as a guide to rest my fingers on, and angle it the way I wanted.

In summary, this is not the machine you want for general grinding but it is great for special purposes. The wheel is too soft for shaping tools, but perfect for touching them up. And that is my need - I shape my cutters with a home-made jig on my 8\\", but once I've mounted them in the shaft of the tool (with CA glue) I have to touch them up free hand often during a session of turning a hollow form from hard wood. I put the Neiko on my lathe bed and do my touch-up, then put it back on the table. Five stars for my purpose, only four in this review as others have different needs.

Best, Jon

product_title: (Discontinued by Manufacturer)
review_body:
Overall this is an excellent pin nailer. It can take 1/2\\" to 1 3/8\\" 23 gauge pins; most others I've seen only handle up to 1\\" pins.

I used this with 1\\" pins for the narrow side of some door trim. All the pins went in smoothly and effortlessly with no bending, and all went in fully. The tip of the pinner's nose has a small no-mar pad, so there's very little risk of damaging any surface as you drive pins. In fact, the pins go in so nicely and the 23-gauge is so fine that they almost disappear - you can hardly see the hole. No need to fill or anything, and you could paint right over the holes.

There is an annoying safety you hold down with your middle fingers so you can press the trigger, and the tab on it digs in and irritates pretty quickly. It can be easily removed so I didn't mark down for this but then you lose that safety feature. On a side note, be careful with pins because occasionally they can horseshoe and pop out nearby - which can be rather unpleasant if your other hand (or thumb) is there.

Finally, it takes several drops of air tool lubricant each day if you don't have a compressor with an in-line lubrication system (and most don't). Often air tools will come with a small tube of lubricant - this did not, so pick some up. It did come with safety goggles though.

Overall I'm very pleased with this pinner - it will really help with the finished look on my projects vs. my larger brad nailer.

product_title: SHOP FOX W1712 1.5-Horsepower 6/12-Inch Combination Disc and Belt Sander
review_headline: A good sander for the money
review_body:
I have read a number of reviews and even went and looked at one of these machines before I made my purchase. And having the unit for a while now I must agree with most of the reviews on key issues for the sander.

First I must say its not a bad machine and I have been rather pleased with the unit. Though it is not a Powermatic, I didn't spend $1200 either, but I do feel its a decent value given the price, quality, and some shortcomings. Shop fox would do very well to make some of these minor improvements and really step up this machine to a better level.

1. The tables are nice and large being made from cast iron. The table on the belt has a feature where the pivot bolts are loosened and the tilting knobs are removed, then the table simply lifts up, out, and off. However there is no positive stop for the 90 degree adjustment, so either trust the degree scale and/or check it with a square. The table can be removed for attaching the work stop fence for flat sanding. I have not tried the work stop fence, I have a drum sander for that operation.

the table for the disc is also nice and large and made from cast iron. It had 2 sets of holes for the pivot, the manual shows a picture that might lead one to believe that the lower of the 2 should be used but I used the upper hole closer to the table surface, it matched the arc for the table tilt knobs. The manual also did not show using the lock nut on the back side of the cap screws used for the table pivot. I installed the cap screws to where the table could pivot and then used the locknuts to lock the cap screw in place. I think this was the intent and it is how I am using it. The table for the disc is not easily removed, but I can replace the paper on the disc without removing the table. This table too has no positive stops for 90 degree adjustment.

Neither table has a T-slot, and this could be useful for attaching jigs and other accessories for operations such as circle sanding, etc. And it is nice that the belt and disc each have their own tables.

2. The enclosed cabinet is indeed a waste of space so I left the back off, placed the unit on a mobile base and made a shelf for the bottom of the unit. I plan on making a small shelf unit to sit inside the base. And since it is on a mobile base the shelf keeps the sides in place and the unit is sturdy. I would not do this if the unit is to be free standing on the floor. The smaller Shop Fox w1676 sander has a door. A nice door and 2 shelves would really help this unit. The rubber feet are not adjustable but this has not been an issue as mine is on a mobile base.

3. Dust collection is a must with a sander and lack of it is a health risk, not to mention its going to get messy. This sander can make a lot of saw dust and that means its working well. I must agree that the plastic dust hood on the belt and disc do indeed leave a lot to be desired. They seem flimsy but have not caused too much concern yet. It is odd that the disc uses a 2\\" hose and the belt uses a 2 1/2\\" hose. I am still working on a suitable setup for dust collection. I envision adapting up the disc hood to 2 1/2\\" right away and running both to a 4\\" quick couple hose connector. If the cabinet wasn't going to be used then Shop Fox could have ran hoses from both the belt and disc inside the cabinet and connected them to a Y and a 4 inch hose connector on the cabinet side much like a jointer would use.

4. Belt tracking has not been an issue on my sander, but I can see where it could be problematic. Included in my little kit of parts was a screwdriver handle with a hole (figured out it was for the belt change lever) and a screwdriver with just a smooth rod (figured out it was for the belt tracking and tension bolt) Not mentioned in the manual but was entertaining to figure out what they were for. If the belt does track off it will cut the plastic dust hood to shreds in a short time. Though I have seen the metal ones get cut up too, its just much faster and less obvious when it happens with the plastic hood. This too is an area that could be improved with some minor tweaks in the engineering. The W1676 seems to have better user friendly tracking using a knob rather than tools. A metal guide or stop could be designed to protect the dust hood should the belt get off track.

5. The on/off switch performs well but does seem to be a bit on the cheap side. I would have preferred a cabinet mounted switch with the more official looking green button red paddle switch. Though the W1676 has a cabinet mounted switch it uses the same on as this sander.

6. Machine speed is 1725 RPM and this works very well. It allows a lot of control over the sanding rate and burns less than my other unit running at 3450 RPM. One interesting observation is the disc spins clockwise. I thought it would take some getting used to but it was not an issue. A friend of mine said isn't that normal? My Shopsmith spins that way.

I like this sander and yes I would buy it again if I were in need of a sander. It does feel like this was a bench mounted sander that was stuck onto a quick cabinet design. I would encourage Shop Fox to consider making some improvements on this machine. It is a good machine and I do recommend it, but it gets 4 out of 5 for me right now.etal ones get cut up too, its just much faster and less obvious when it happens with the plastic hood. This too is an area that could be improved with some minor tweaks in the engineering. The W1676 seems to have better user friendly tracking using a knob rather than tools. A metal guide or stop could be designed to protect the dust hood should the belt get off track.

5. The on/off switch performs well but does seem to be a bit on the cheap side. I would have preferred a cabinet mounted switch with the more official looking green button red paddle switch. Though the W1676 has a cabinet mounted switch it uses the same on as this sander.

I like this sander and yes I would buy it again if I were in need of a sander. It does feel like this was a bench mounted sander that was stuck onto a quick cabinet design. product_title: Bosch 1594K 3-1/4" Planer with Carrying Case,
review_body:
In light of the other thorough reviews here, I will just add the following for those on the fence between this and the festool HL850.

I am a festool believer, and I use their system, but decided to go with the bosch planer because I am unlikely to use a planer to cut rabbets, and am not likely to want to use the festool shaping cutter heads. If you need either of those features, the festool is possibly a better choice. However, if you need to mostly plane with flat blades, and will be using this to level boards, the Bosch has several advantages:

1. Much lower cost, for essentially the same flat planing performance.
2. much cheaper blades, which means when working with rough lumber, it is less critical to use a metal detector to check for all nails/staples. Additionally, the blades are reversible, so for $11 you get 2 uses of them. Also, they are carbide, which makes them hold up to dirty lumber better (grit dulls steel faster than carbide)
3. Bosch is not a specialty brand as much as festool is, this makes it easier to locate blades, not only on amazon, but also at the local tool store. Sometimes you don't want to wait a day for shipping if you nick a blade in the middle of a project.

I can't comment on the angle stop's efficacy as I haven't used it yet, but I suspect that I would want to add on larger guide plates, as one of the other commenters suggested, to give it better stability.

product_title: Makita 6952 2.3 Amp Impact Driver
review_body:
We purchased this tool after searching for a small impact driver with a cord. This seems to be the only one out there, but it is well worth it. We used it to screw down an entire 20x30 deck and never once had to worry about battery charge. Impact drivers have revolutionized the art of driving screws, and the technology works very well for cordless tools. We have several of the Makita 14.4v impact drivers, but when it comes to a big job, get a corded tool.

When it comes to driving stainless screws, this tool is amazing. Usually with a long stainless screw, if the charge peters out and the screw doesn't fully drive, the next attempt will either strip out the head or break off the shank of the screw, which can lead to no end of troubles on expensive decking systems. Using this tool guarantees that you will always have all the power you need to fully drive the longest screws all the while maintaining a good bite on the screw. This tool also drives the new Simpson framing lag screws very well, even without predrilling. Again, it just keeps bringing the power to do the work.

Awesome tool.

product_title: Gerber Myth Folding Saw [31-001167]
review_headline: Great saw for deer hunters in climbing stands
review_body:
I've always had a Gerber saw in my hunting bag but my previous one succumbed to fate of a desperate man on a hunting trip last year. I needed a branch on the tree next to my stand gone and I couldn't reach it from my stand. My idea was to saw down a young sapling and zip-tie my folding saw to the end of it and use it as a pole saw. This worked great until I pinched the saw in the branch and bent the blade until it broke. I got the limb down and my saw back, but it was missing an inch off the end of the blade.

This year I added the Gerber Myth folding saw to my hunting pack and I don't see how any hunter could go without one. A tree with numerous branches is impossible to climb in a climbing treestand without a saw. Tiny little limbs will be the death of you if you think green oak branches are easy to snap with your hands. The Gerber Myth saw is the nominal size for a cargo pocket or side pocket on a hunting pack. The blade locks closed and open, and requires you to push the button in order for it unlock. This will prevent any accidental openings and closings that could injure your fingers. It has a really grippy handle that was easy to hang on to even with gloves on a windy, cold morning in the 2012 Georgia deer season.

The 6 3/4″ SK5 carbon steel blade has coarse and fine teeth. They say this makes it idea for bone and wood. I haven't tried it yet on bone, but it made short work of the numerous limbs I had to cut while climbing both oak and pine trees in a Summit Viper and Ole' Man Multi-Vision Climbing deerstand. The only real qualm I had with this saw is it didn't include a sheath so I could permanently attach it to my stand. This isn't that big of a deal because It easily fits in my pants pocket, but it's just something to think about.

product_title: Shop Fox D2730 3-Inch Cross Sliding Vise
review_headline: Good vice for the money - precise enough for most...
review_body:
Arrived in good condition and knew out of the box it would need cleaning and fixes (per reviews here).

Good: A lot of product for $50. x, y and a vice. If one views it as a \\"I paid so little because it's 95% done\\" then its quite a good deal. If one is looking for ready to use out of the box, look elsewhere. Also this is not a $500 vice either - so the precision is limited.

Needs: it had a few bits of metal on it, else grease was on many painted surfaces - however there was no rust so the greasing worked.

1. Both screws did not get the finely engineered mounts (keep costs down?) - thus I added 3 washers - outside bottom, inner and outer on top - this reduced the friction and soon will be replaced with bushings or bearings. The upper screw has a machined shoulder for the inner washer to sit on, whereas the lower screw rests on a squashed last thread.

2. To fix the lower layer slop, the acme screw carrier/threaded shaft needs to be screwed in somehow. In the current design, a tall cylinder is tapped and the screw goes through the lower half, and the upper half of the cylinder is narrower and \\"catches\\" a hold in the x/y carrier. Because it is not screwed in to that layer, it rocks when the screw has axial forces applied. Simply flip the vice over and slide it - the \\"catch\\" wiggles and the end of the acme screw flops around in the end. Once I get this fixed I'll post some pics.

3. The hand cranks did not turn smoothly - I unscrewed the finger hold of the crank handle out, put that threaded end in a drill, sprayed some graphite in the gap and ran the drill for 20 seconds or so - while flexing and tweaking the handle. The finger holds on the crank handles spin much smoother now.

Updated: I used the vice for some woodwork and it tends to be \\"bindy\\" - not sure if from the chips catching in the ways or the threads - need to look into that.

Also being an XY vice - these are too tall for smallerdrill presses. I have a HF 8\\" drill press and the vice is mounted to the drill press base and the table swung aside. If more height is needed, being the drill press base is bolted to the benchtop I could secure the vice to the bench and swing the head over to gain about an inch..

I very well got my money's worth for $50 bucks. 4 stars because I would have gladly paid $15 more for the above 3 fixes to be done at the factory. But the engineers and product folks know this.

I have a pretty decent electric hammer drill, but I was using some of the cheap, silver off-brand drill bits to make holes. The bits would last maybe 4-10 holes, but seemed to make holes a tiny bit larger than advertised, meaning my Tapcon screws weren't getting a good bite, and some were stripping their threads and spinning in the pre-drilled holes!

These Bosch bits--which are longer (6\\" total) and stronger (especially the cutting head)--lasted much longer, and only wore out after some agressive drilling that must've hit some rebar along the way. Also, the holes they drilled were perfect for the two common sizes of Tapcon screws--5/32\\" and 3/16\\". When I drilled in the Tapcons, my handheld power drill could use all it's power to push, and not spin the Tapcons. A VERY good bite, and one I'm sure will outlast the walls of the house!

The bag these bits come in is a nice, thick plastic, meaning you can toss the bits in the bag inside your drill case, or a toolbox, and not worry about the bits grinding or scratching other tools.

product_title: Energy, Inc. 5000-C TED (The Energy Detective) 5000 by TED 5000-C
review_body:
I just got my TED and have been running it only a short time but I do like it. I've found a few interesting data already, e.g. my TV takes less energy then a light bulb to run but my Comcast box is a hog.

The set up was very simple if you read the directions and watch the video. Of course if you are afraid of installing something in the circuit breaker box, then this device may not be for you. Total time to set up was about an hour which includes installing the device and configuring it on my PC. I watched the video and read the directions last night so the 1 hour estimate may be a little low. Let's give total install time, including software and configuration, about 90 minutes. The video is only 5 minutes but I watched it twice. I followed the instructions on installing the MTU and it was easy. Total time did not exceed 15 minutes. Skill required to install the MTU is very low.

The software was very easy to install and the connection to the gateway and the MTU was simply...no advanced skills required there either (although I am a software engineer so I can't really judge for the average PC user). The only problem I had came when I decided to upgrade the firmware. I had set the device password and after upgrading the firmware, it would not accept the password. I had to reset the gateway device by unpluging it. It was a bit of a scare. I suggest if you plan to upgrade the firmware that you do it before any other configuration.

I was considering giving it only 3 stars because the wireless display leaves much to be desired. It will dim out after only 30 seconds. It appears as though the battery life is VERY limited (I do mean VERY limited) so they do everything they can to extend it. You can adjust the time to dim and the amount it dims in the dashboard software but dimming the display makes it almost unreadable. The device almost needs to be plugged in all the time. The wireless is also limited in range. It often has no connection when I am downstairs in my home. I mostly use my PC for graphing anyway so the wireless display is not getting used much. Knowing what I know now, I probably would have saved the money and not bought the display. However, it does provide a nice check to make sure that my PC is working correcty.

Bottom line: Set up for me was easy requiring no special skills and the data are rolling in after less than 2 hours (including time to write this review). I will update if my opinion ever changes.

Update: I've been using the device for about a year now. It does have some bugs as others have noted. The biggest problem occurs when you lose power and the historical data are wiped out. Be sure to save the data often if you want to see long term or seasonal trends. It also occasionally loses data for no reason at all that I can tell. Network connection can be flaky. It will stop communicating and require a reset. As others have said, it requires some work to keep everything going. If you expect to set it and forget it, this is not the device for you. I down graded to three stars because of the problems.

product_title: Shop Fox D4088 Lathe Attachment for Drill Press
review_body:
First, I'm just breaking into wood turning - I figured I would get this guy to see if I was any good at it, let alone if I liked it or not. The box Amazon shipped was in good condition, the box inside that was beat up, torn open, missing parts (nuts to the bolts that hold this to the drill press) and included extra washers(?). I'm sure I can hit the local Ace to compensate for the missing nuts, although from further investigation I can't see how this would work. It's pretty simple system, a cast iron bar that bolts to the drill press base, a 2nd smaller bar that screws into the main bar and with the 12\\" tool rest that screws into that - the problem is that the screws that hold this together stick through the bottom of the main. So... unless your drill press has enough room and/or slots for the main bolts and and the screw that stick through the bottom - it's not going to be level/flat against the base. Even with the 'extra' washers, the screw still sticks through the bar. I don't see how this would work, I'm going to be returning this for sure.

*IF* this did work - it looks as though it may work okay. The metal is solid/heavy iron, there is the live center which doesnt spin that well, but should do the job. There is the spur and screw centers - the screw center is literally a screw with a small nut on it, at first it just looked like a screw glued to a piece of metal, but it's not (I hope) - granted Im new at this, although Im not sure what that screw will actually be able to hold anything at 1000+ RPM. The spur center looks descent enough to do the job how ever.

Over all, there isnt much to this guy, the engineering could have been done a lot better thats for sure. I've got the Skill 3320-02 Drill Press ([[ASIN:B003LSSS0W SKIL 3320-02 120-Volt 10-Inch Drill Press]]) and this does not fit it with the screw sticking out the bottom. In the very least the Amazon description is way off with the press just needing a \\"through hole in the table\\".

product_title: Bosch Random Orbit Sander with Carrying Bag
review_body:
I have most types of hand power sanders but did not have a random orbit sander. I needed to remove the paint from a wide trim board and was looking for something that was less work than scraping, did not use chemicals, was faster than an inline sander, and not as prone to the spontaneous loss of control of a belt sander.

This tool was perfect. I researched a number of brands, ranging from $29 to over $100, and the Bosch reviews and feature set seemed to be not only what I needed but best in class. It is quieter than my other sanders, and does a moderate job of collecting dust in the attached box. After using it that way for a while I hooked up my shop vac to the dust port and it collected nearly all of the dust - should have done it that way from the start. The only criticism I have is that it took some fiddling with adapters and the included adapter to hook the vac up to the dust port.

The sander is very smooth in operation and feels powerful. It felt like just the right weight to be easily operable but solid. I am glad I got the variable speed model, as tuning the speed adds one more way of controlling the job outcome (besides the amount of time sanding and sand paper grit and type).

I recommend the Bosch and would get it again. Next up is to see how well it sands oak stairs - I would like to avoid renting and using an edge sander if possible. Not so much for the price ($29 for 4 hours locally or $49 for the day) but because it is a bigger, heavier and less controllable tool.

product_title: Gerber E-Z Out Skeleton Knife 06751
review_headline: A good, American Knife at a great price
review_body:
I've owned a number of Gerber EZ-out knives over the last 10 years - They've always been sharp, sturdy and value-priced. I actually paid close to $60 for my first one from a local outdoors shop, so I was tickled to find this one for $25 on Amazon. As a commercial sailor and recreational boater, knives like this have a shorter than average lifespan with me. It is noteworthy that no Gerber of mine has ever failed due to a fault in manufacturing.
The handle feels a little thinner than the older models, light and rigid - similar to Zytel. The familiar raised rubber ridges are still there, and provide good grip and control in wet conditions. I like the shape of the handle and the spring bar detent at 90 degrees open.
The knife I received came in a small cardboard box - the way knives used to. I hate battling through clam pack, so that was a nice change. It was a little different than the one in the picture, but I like it. Mine has a black spring bar/lock, and came with a lanyard hole at the butt.
The base of the blade still reads 'Portland OR', which is nice considering the number that say 'China'. Factory edge is pretty good - actually quite sharp - but has some burrs that need attention.
All in all, an excellent 50/50 locking knife at this price. I may even buy another to keep as a spare.

product_title: Kreg NZ03-B Drawer Mounting Brackets
review_headline: Works OK but a pair of 5 gallon paint sticks work better
review_body:
I bought these with the Kreg NZ03 Magnetic Drawer Slide Mounting Tool to help replace some old roller slides with ball bearing full extension drawer slides. I found that these worked fine if you had plenty of clearance but did not work well on bottom drawers where you had trim as you could not get them front flush. This is where I discovered that a 5 gallon paint stick has the same height. I simply pushed the paint stick all the way in to the back of the drawer and under the cabinet inside mounting bracket, placed the drawer on top with a slight bit exposed and put in the screws as the drawer was level side to side, leaving room to adjust with the adjuster slots as needed.

I am giving this tool a 3 review because it will not solve all of your needs. I think a design flaw is that the rear part of support that goes under the inside mounting bracket is too short. It should be able to almost support itself and the drawer without necessarily being clamped (understanding that it would be recommended to be clamped of course). I did 12 drawers and out of the 12 I used this tool on only 5. Once I discovered the paint stick method it was quicker and cleaner.

All in all, I would not buy this again if I had to do it all over but it does work in some cases.

Indeed, higher decibel-reducing earplugs can be quite thick and unpleasant to put in your ear, but these 3M ones are so soft that I've actually slept in them, and very comfortably so! Barely able to feel them inside my ear when my head hit the pillow, so if you have noisy neighbors or just don't sleep very soundly, they work great for such occasions.

Overall, a very comfortable, moderately excellent noise-reducing earplug. Recommended.

review_headline: Extremely handy, even for home use
review_body:
I got this for one door in my house that is the only one I don't feel very secure about. I wasn't sure it would work because none of the reviews I read mentioned the thickness of the metal so, for all I knew, it wouldn't fit between the door and frame.

Well, the good news is that it fit perfectly on that particular door. The metal piece is just inside of 1/16\\" thick. That's really all you need to know, aside from what has already been mentioned by reviewers and in the description of the item. It seems extremely sturdy.

So, now this door which only has a doorknob lock, feels really super secure. Sure, I suppose somebody very strong could kick it in, but now they cannot just stick a credit card into the space and dislodge the doorknob lock. I can pull on the door until the cows come home and it does not budge one millimeter.

It took me a few minutes to figure it out, although it did come with an 8x11\\" sheet of paper with instructions. For some reason, it just didn't make sense to me but when I finally put it in there, exactly as instructed, I saw for myself how well it works. It's not that it is complicated. It's just that I read the instructions and found myself feeling confused as to how THAT would make it secure the door. So just read the instruction and do what it says. You will see for yourself that, however it does it, it really does secure the door.

I'm very happy with this item and almost wish I had gotten the two-pack for a small savings.

if you have a stack of sortainers or systainers then this thing is a dream. the casters are extremely smooth. the connection from the cart to the sort/systainers is made with little rubber clips which seem a little flimsy at first, but they get the job done. it also comes with an extra set in case they break or you lose them. it's fairly easy to take the cart off and put a stack of sort/systainers back on.
i have a stack of two sortainers and a systainer on top that i take to most jobs. i keep these on the cart and can stack other non-festool tools on top of the whole thing while moving things around the jobsite. it's not good for stairs and whatnot, but it rolls well over a variety of flat surfaces (carpet, pavers, asphalt, wood, etc.). nice time saver.

review_headline: Chinese junk?  Not just a ship
review_body: Some things you can't tell until it arrives at your house:  the part that connects the pump to your tire is made of plastic.  Remember the bike pump you used as a kid?  It's connector was metal.  Good reason.  This part failed (for me) broke exactly 30 seconds into its first use, rendering the whole thing worthless.  Also, think about where the switch that turns this on is located.  If you plug this into an AC outlet, you have to drag out the DC connector so that you can get to the switch. Now exactly where is the switch?  It's inside the back of the unit.  You can't see the gauge, and turn the thing on at the same time, well, not without getting on your hands and knees, if you are filling a car tire or something else you cant place on a table.  It's what I would consider a design flaw.  The gauge also is a bit vague, as commented on other reviews. The one I received was marked on PSI (10 pound increments) and "atmospheres" in case - well I'm not sure for what.  Basketballs?  So, I returned it.  You may find it works for you.

Yesterday, while working while wearing these gloves, I did have to briefly dip one hand into icy water.

At first, it seemed like the gloves really were waterproof: I felt some coldness but no wetness as a result of that action.

But then I went inside and took off the gloves. Instead of drying out, the glove that had gotten wet stayed sodden into the afternoon, long after all of the other clothing I had worn out in the snow had dried.

This morning, I felt the outside of the glove and it was dry, so I put it on. Oh no! It wasn't dry at all. All of the moisture had wicked to the inside of the glove, which was soaking wet.

I've had it on a radiator for a few hours now, and the inside is still quite damp.

Moisture wicked to the inside of the glove, where it remains trapped? That's the opposite of waterproof, as far as I'm concerned.

Also, as others have said (wish I had read more reviews before buying), these run small in the hand area and long in the fingers. They are also very stiff at first but do stretch out a bit as you work while wearing them.

product_title: Makita 9404 8.8-Amp 4-by-24-Inch Variable Speed Belt Sander with Cloth Dust Bag
review_headline: It may be better to get more power.
review_body: I did not buy this 8.8 amp model, but the 11 amp non-variable speed 9403.  I've used it about twelve hours now.  With a forty grit belt it is easy to bog down the 11 amp model.  I was very thankful I bought it instead of the variable speed 9404 with only 8.8 amps, which is more in line with the 3 x 21 belt sanders.  As to the variable speed, I have not missed it one bit.  As a woodworker and former contractor I have over forty years of experience with power tools and have found that the most common thing to go bad on any tool is the variable speed control.  Perhaps these are better, I hope so for all who buy it.  If you need to slow a sander down, why not just use a belt that is not so coarse?  The 9403 is a beefy sander that allows no mistakes.  But if you follow good practise and start the sander before it contacts the wood, then contact gently, and then lift off while it is still turning, you will be fine.  I gave this one four stars as I had to give it a rating to be able to say this.  If you can afford it, one would be wise to get a small belt sander like the little Porter Cable mouse, and then a four inch with some beef to it.  Bottom line: if you are running finer belts, I'm sure the 8.8 amp is fine, but if you want to hog off some wood, go for the 11 amp.

I purchased the Freezerators from the Nebraska Furniture Mart in 2007. Within 6 months the compressor froze up and I lost over $1,000 worth of meat and food! I had it stocked with 2 turkeys for the Holidays, Steaks for a final fall grill, a Ham for a birthday party and tons of chicken, hamburger and pork chops bought in bulk.
I was in shock. It took 3 trips to figure out the problem and fix it. The fix was under warranty but the CONTENTS of the freezer were not! I still had receipts for the meat and pictures of us taking out the thawed, spoiling meats. Whirlpool could have cared less.
But God Bless Bob Batt (NFM exec. and grandson of founder) He sent me a check to replace all of the food with a personal note. He didn't 'have' to do it, but they know how to conduct a great business. They value their customers. Mr. Batt researched the product and found out they stopped ordering them from whirlpool shortly after I bought it. Apparently the problem with the compressor is in every one of the freezerators! Some break down right away, some within a few years. Whirlpool should have recalled it from the market, as they were well informed of these problems.

I will never purchase a Whirlpool product again...but I am an NFM customer for life!

product_title: ZAP Enforcer Stun Flashlight
review_headline: Nice piece of equipment that could use a couple tweaks
review_body:
Recently purchased this device basically for checking out those odd noises in the night. The flashlight works great! It is about the same amount of light as my 4 D cell mag light but a bit more dispersed. You get a slightly wider beam without the dark ring being quite as large as it would be with a Mag Light. However, the beam is not adjustable as far as I can tell. Or maybe I'm too scared to put my hand near the front of this thing :) The device seems heavy enough to be compared to a Mag Light as well, however it is weighted toward the front where as a Mag Light is heavier toward the rear.

You get three settings for the flashlight which allows you to conserve battery. The strobe feature is really cool and effective at disorienting friends and family. However, it is not reliable. It says to hold down the button for ten seconds and then release for strobe effect. Well...about 4 sec will do, most of the time. Most of the time it works fine, sometimes it just turns on the flashlight on high beam, and occasionally a faint strobe projects prior to releasing the button. So it's not near reliable enough to count on if you were thinking of using this feature to disorient an intruder.

The light up display is pretty cool. You can tell how much time you have left on each flashlight setting, including when the strobe is on. You can easily read the screen and tell how many 'zaps' you have left, I'm not sure what the unit of measurement is though. The only problem is that the screen is so brightly back lit that it will light up the hallway you are in with a faint blue glow. Not great for sneaking around the house. I've learned to carry it so that it covers this screen but this makes the buttons more awkward to push should I need to do so in a hurry.

I'm not sure how to rate the stun feature as I haven't had to use it. It works, sounds scary, certainly sent my dog running for a safe corner to hide in and she was in the next room. IfI could, I would separate the buttons a bit more. The flashlight and stun button are pretty close. I have another model that used a switch on the top and a button on the other side for stun and I prefer that.

Overall: Not bad. I feel I can depend on the flashlight and stun features and the weight gives you that extra security that comes with products like mag lights. Some of the features could use adjustment, but their deficiencies can be compensated for with the exception of the randomly functioning strobe.

I don't feel this is going to last very long, as my experiences with this type of plastic is that it always seems to crack and/or break after awhile. This type of plastic might be fine for their pocket hole jigs and tools like that, because they don't flex nor bend. This tool has a lot of flex where the saw attaches.

The ruler is quality aluminum, but you have to drill your own hole if you want to hang it up.
(it's a miracle it showed up in one straight piece, because, as usual, Amazon dropped it in a big box with a single sheet of brown paper for packing and drop kicked it to me via UPS)

Overall, it works fine so far, but all the little nuts and screws seem amateurish, and the mounting technology for the saw itself seems like an afterthought.

By the way, the DeWalt cordless saw doesn't mount very well as the front of the shoe is raised (beveled up).
A Ryobi mounts very well. I haven't tried any others yet.

5 stars for concept
4 stars for functionality
1 star for quality of materials.

review_headline: Great saw, ergonomic with plenty of power!
review_body: Great price for a powerful saw. The saw's plug is a 20 amp type with one prong turned sideways, so I took a heavy-duty (#12 wire) extension cord, cut off the plug and replaced it with a 20 amp receptacle box. That solved the \\"it won't plug into my extension cord\\" problem. I could have changed the plug on the saw, but I didn't want to void the warranty. It did throw my houses 20 amp breaker several times while cutting, but that's not too surprising considering the work it was doing.  The dual handles made manipulating it easy. I cut out a window hole in an 8\\" thick solid concrete wall by cutting from the inside and then the outside. I first drilled corner holes so I could see to line up the cuts. Inside, I cut dry and used an exhaust fan with a 12\\" diameter flexible hose (extendable to 20') to pull out the dust and that took most of the dust out but made quite a cloud outside--use a garden hose if you have close neighbors (a shop vac will NOT keep up with the dust, I tried that first). Outside, I hooked up a garden hose to which I had added a shutoff valve near the end so I could control the water flow speed, and that stopped all dust, though it did create a river of milky water--make sure you have somewhere for the water to drain if you do this! I plan to use it on several other projects, so that's why I bought instead of  renting (it would have cost me about $130 to rent a similar saw for the time it took me). Overall a great saw for an unbelievable price!

review_headline: Big and bright - simply an amazing light

Since early July 2012 I have purchased three of these impressive Maglite D cell LED flashlights here an Amazon: one in camouflage (for the car) as well as one in silver and one in black (both for the house).

Perhaps this is something that you too should consider doing just in case an unexpected emergency comes knocking at your door some day?

Since the two D cell and three D cell versions of this LED Maglite essentially cost the same (between $20.00 and $30.00 depending on the color chosen), I personally feel that the three D cell version is the better buy (longer run-time with three instead of only two batteries), as long as you have room available for the longer/bigger light.

product_title: Inova X1 LED Flashlight
review_headline: Old tech, with much better AA lights available-- read for links
review_body:
At one time this flashlight was more competitive, but these days many flashlights are available at a similar price point (or lower) with much better specifications.

This light is solidly built compared to older flashlights, but modern flashlight makers such as Fenix make even more durable lights out of aircraft-grade aluminum and other materials. The build on this light is decent but not stellar by modern standards; it only for example offers water resistant construction (I believe the listing to be in error on this), while more modern competing lights offer 1PX8 complete waterproofing to two meters or more. Competing lights also tend to offer more brightness levels/modes (which aids in runtime and preservation of night vision), better max brightness, optional ability to take higher-powered 14500 batteries, and other features.

Some competing more modern 1 X AA lights in the same price band with better features include the [[ASIN:B005GMF0TS Olight i2]], [[ASIN:B0035H9B5U ITP A2 EOS]], [[ASIN:B005GW8UC2 Fenix E11]], [[ASIN:B003U0ARL4 Fenix LD15]], [[ASIN:B004UG51OK JETBeam BA10]], and [[ASIN:B004UA61RW 4Sevens Quark MiNi AA]]. This list is not exhaustive, but hopefully browsing this selection will convince you that you can get far more for your money than with the Inova X1. It's not bad; it's simply an older design with older tech, and not competitive today.

product_title: Vega PRO 50 Table Saw Fence System: 42-Inch Fence Bar, 50-Inch to Right
review_headline: New life for an old saw
review_body:
I'm just a homeowner that likes to do as much of my own work as possible. I'd say I'm an decent intermediate woodworker and cabinet maker, not a pro by any means. I'm in the middle of remodeling a kitchen and bathroom and will be making some new base cabinets among other things. Stock fences have always been a problem for me so, I decided to take the plunge and buy the Vega fence. I picked up a beautiful old Craftsman 10\\" saw last year for $100 (model 113.29920, made in 1956 according to Sears). You know, the ones with the nice heavy cast iron table and side extensions (they don't make 'em like that anymore). So, this fence was more than double the price of my saw, and so far it's worth every penny!!

It took me a couple of hours to set-up from the time I opened the box but that's no fault of the Vega fence. I was proceeding very deliberately so as not to screw it up. After removing the stock front fence rail, the Vega front tube brackets lined right up on the existing holes. I only had to drill two 5/16\\" holes in my table for the back fence mounting tube. They definitely thought this design out and it shows. Once you square the fence up to a miter slot, you crank down on four heavy socket head machine screws to secure the fence to the very solid head. There's plenty of adjustments all around to fine tune the clearance above the bed (about 1/16\\" seemed to work for me) and to get the scale zeroed out. When you have everything set and cranked down, I can't see things being able to move out of adjustment. Every piece is very solid, the fence rides smoothly on the tubes and all adjustments are easily accessible.

The unit arrived by UPS Ground and was very well packaged and protected in a heavy cardboard box, stapled securely and further protected with heavy cardboard spacers and 2x4 wood blocking inside the shipping box. I agree that the instructions leave a lot to be desired. But, it's a very logical set-up and not that hard to scope out. If I can do it, I think most anybody with a reasonable degree of tool sense can do it just as well or better. Love that it's made in the USA!

All in all it was a fun afternoon and now my old saw makes dead-on cuts including ripping an 8' 2x4 just to see how things worked - right on the money the entire length. The scale is pretty easy to fine-tune to a high degree of accuracy if you take your time. The micro-adjustment is a very nice feature and works smoothly after a little break-in time (a little stiff at first but limbered up nicely after only a couple of uses). I am very pleased with the sturdy construction and ease of use. I hope this is helpful to anyone considering this fence. I would buy it again and would recommend to a friend. No more dust in my nose and lungs and all over my workbench and floor, this product really saves me time on clean up! I love this item and when I use up the Other side of this sponge, I will order more! Thanks SANDLUTIONS Vacuu-Sponge for a great product to save my health and save me time in unnecessary clean up! product_title: Hitachi EC89 4-Gallon Portable Electric Twin Stack Air Compressor
review_body: I just opened my EC89 about 2 weeks ago having bought this at least a year ago. Initial start of the compressor was fine... building pressure and all that. I turned it off, and didn't get back to it a week later and the thermal reset kept kicking in. I called Hitachi Customer Service and he asked if I was on an extension chord... blah blah blah .. tried it without an extension chord ... works the same; thermal switch kept kicking in. But before calling Hitachi, it was obvious the switch was kicking in due to \\"stress\\". Stress? ... yeah .. like it's lacking the \\"power\\" to keep the compressor going. Me knowing somethings here and there, I asked the rep. if there were any problems with the starter cap? He said \\"no\\". Then today, I find a comment on this product on the internet.. indeed they do have a problem with the design. Apparently, the initial starter cap. was 40 microfarads and to over come the starting issue is to replace the starter cap. with a 60 microfarad capacitor. Apparently also, a new version has the 60 microfarad cap. I will inquire again with Hitachi Tech Support about this issue to see if they will fix this for me. Hitachis Tech Support said there is no issue with the unit nor are there any recalls; so thumbs down to them. I don't know what version of the EC89 I have, but I asked Lowes if they will take it back and they said they will as long as they are still selling the unit. Coincidentally, they were still selling the unit. It has been a year since I got this unit and I'm assuming the \\"new\\" EC89s probably were designed with a higher rated starter cap. I was in luck; returned it to Lowes, got store credit and spent an additional $150 for an assumed better compressor \\"DeWalt D55146\\". I bought it this afternoon, got home this evening, and tried the unit out by plugging into the same circuit plus an extension chord... AND IT WORKS! .. AGAIN AND AGAIN ... That's the solution; if you can't get the Hitachi compressor working,,. get a different manufacturer's and a better overall spec. one. What annoyed me with this whole thing is Hitachi Tech Support (same guy I talked to last week) refuse to say the \\"new and improved EC89 comes with a higher rated starter cap...\\". He's paid not to admit it. This is one 'X' on Hitachi and I may never buy any of their things again.  I had no choice to give it a 1 star as reviews need at least 1 star... ;).  Sorry Hitachi... but you failed me as I am a paying customer.

review_body:
I'm not sure why people think of Black & Decker as a somewhat inferior brand compared to others. I have used their products for a long time and have never been disappointed.

This is a great drill, and its smaller size is actually an advantage for me as you get portability, but you still get the power (I was actually surprised at how powerful this drill is).

Pros:
*Power - You will be pleasantly surprised!
*24-position clutch - Works as advertised. This also allows you to use the drill on more delicate items
*100-Piece Accessory Kit - This has a lot of the essential accessories to do most of your DIY projects at home. The great thing is they are actually pretty sturdy and are not of cheap quality.
*Price - Comparable drills from other brands are a lot more expensive.
*20-volt battery - Most are 18-volt or less,
*Size - Makes this drill very portable.

Cons
*Case - The case is horrible! The drill is floating in the case, without any fasteners holding it securely. Also the accessory holders could have been done better.
Size - While not a con for me personally, this could be problematic if you want to use large drill bits, as the chuck head is quite small.

I haven't used it till the battery drains fully, but so far it seems to hold the charge well.

review_body: This is a great wrench for the price - under $12 right now and it's on Prime. I bought this for use on my homebrew kegerator equipment. This wrench expands to about 1.4\\", not the full 1.5\\", but it's enough for these applications. Homebrew and keg supply shops sell specialty wrenches just for these nuts, but they are \\"unitaskers\\" and not much cheaper than this Tekton wrench, and since it's adjustable, you can use it on lots of other tasks - any size nut under 1.5\\". At 12\\" you get a lot of leverage, which is useful even on small nuts that are hard to loosen. It's made in China, but the quality is good. I'm sure there's better wrenchs out there, but the thin foam grip is good and it holds it's width well after you set it. If you're a homebrewer, I'd recommend getting this along with a [[ASIN:B000NPPC78 TEKTON 21561 7/8-Inch Combination Wrench]] for your corny keg posts.

product_title: CREE 40434 X-Tactical ATE0C2L007 Ultra-Bright CREE LED Tactical Aluminum Flashlight
review_body:
The first review below was for the first copy of this light that I'd used for many months without any trouble to speak of. I liked it, especially for the price I paid, but it fell off my chest rig and got lost forever somewhere out there in the woods. In a million years I suppose it'll be worth a fortune. Anyway, I ordered a replacement and the new one is junk; faulty circuitry I suspect. It exhibits an intermittent failure problem. Once in a while and usually when I'm doing something important, the light begins to cut out or fade to very dim, and sometimes strobe at a rapid cyclic rate. Tapping, shaking and button pressing don't seem to effect the problem one way or the other and, for reasons unknown, the light will start running normally again on it's own after a couple of minutes.
The long and the short of it: my new copy of this light can't be counted on and I can no longer recommend this light. Two stars because it still runs, mostly, and if it quits you could use it for a halibut fishing weight or something.

FIRST REVIEW -- I use this light primarily for fox hunting as my scanning light. For the money it's a great little light. Output is plenty if you're running a 17hmr like I am. Mine has a tight, clean \\"sweet spot\\" with a useful amount of flood around the peripheral area which makes a good balance of throw and flood. You'll get eyes shining back at 200 yards and clear target acquisition at 140 or so; about as far as you should ever be shooting fox with that round anyway. Battery life is good for intermittent call and scan usage and I get three nights of use from a set of batts in this way. Naturally your mileage will vary. The filter caps are nice to have if you want to run such a thing (I only use red) and they stay on the light when you put them there. The switch features are a bit odd but big deal; it isn't hard to use. The battery indicator light doesn't suit me because it's too bright. If you set the thing down and walk away from it you can see it a surprisingly long way off. A wrap or two of electricians tape fixed that for me though. This light has held up well over two years of regular use and because of its small size and output it's great for foxing and trapping uses and it has been the demise of many a fur bearing varmint as such. If I could give it four and a half stars that would be just right I think.can see it a surprisingly long way off. A wrap or two of electricians tape fixed that for me though. review_body:
I like the adjustable ems. The spot ratio is pretty decent as well. I'm happy with the overall bang for the buck. Even though it really looks and feels generic, it gets the job done well. It even comes with a little holster type bag.

I wish there was a pocket on it or the bag to hold the probe when not using it. I also wish it used \\"AA\\" or \\"AAA\\" batteries instead of a 9-volt since the \\"AA\\" and \\"AAA\\" batteries are a little more common and easier to find in different varieties.

**UPDATE**
The battery that came with this product finally died. When I tried to replace the battery, the battery cover wouldn't close all the way and popped back open slightly. What I found out is that today's 9-volt batteries have more squared edges which makes the battery a hair bigger. This slight difference doesn't conform with the battery cover's rounded inside and that is what prevents the cover from closing. The battery cover, by the way, is the black piece under the trigger. Right now, I think I will need to figure out a way to keep the cover closed or get a new IR thermometer that doesn't have this problem.

review_body:

My second gripe is also part of one of my favorite features. The saw blade can be swapped out for a file. Which is great, since there aren't many uses for a wood blade at a power plant. However, the lock that holds the file/sawblade doesn't lock in very tightly and can release the file when first opening. I'm sure it could be fixed pretty easily and probably isn't a very common problem. I love having the choice of 2 blades (both of which are super sharp). The lockback device is very easy to use. The wire cutters seem to be pretty durable, cuts through lock wire very easily. Great product! Money very well spent!

UPDATE: After 6 months of regular use, I am much less enthused about the Surge. As an every day work tool, it has way more options than I need. Getting it out of the sheath while wearing gloves is overly difficult. I use the screwdriver more than anything, and it's one of the more difficult tools to open. And the same screwdriver hits the tip of the pliers which makes it difficult to close. When the tool does close, it has a nasty pinch point which gave me a nice blood blister on the palm of my hand. That is when I ordered a Skeletool and retired the Surge to my glove box.
