That summer, I redid my windows and door frames on a good sized two story house. I used it from morning until it got dark for about two months straight. I could not think of a power tool I had gotten in a long time that came close to the versatility and sheer usefulness of that tool.

The only problems with my first one were that it was a single speed (11,000 RPM; Chicago now makes a faster single speed one) and the part where the accessories attach did not have the raised parts that went into the small holes on the blades near the center. That meant that it occasionally slipped unless I tightened the bolt with an Allen wrench so tight it was scary, but it did not come close to stripping.

It may seem unusual that I am reviewing the wrong tool, but I was so impressed with it that I went out and bought this multi speed model. It does everything the first one does and more. It is larger and more powerful, but not unwieldy. Blade attachment is easier and they remain in place among a good choice of positions. It comes with a nice case, but it could have been designed better for storing the power chord.

Since I bought mine, I've tried a variety of attachments, and have a few that I'm sure I will need but have not used yet. Nevertheless, it's not a tool that just sits on a shelf. I probably use at as often as an electric drill, which is saying a lot in the power tool world.

The advantage of a multi speed model is that it works well for sanding at lower speeds when appropriate and at higher cutting speeds when needed. It has a similar speed range to the best on the market.

Usually when I see a tool that claims to do everything, it's a gimmick and either I would never come close to using all the attachments or the tool doesn't measure up to what I saw on TV. This one was different. It exceeded my expectations in every way.

One attachment worked well to dig out silicone caulking from around doors and windows so they could be redone properly. It also served to scrape off flaking paint easily and thoroughly. There is some risk of gouging, but I haven't found anything better for that application.

Where it really saved more than its price in a single use was for plunge cutting. If you need to cut off a section of wood that needs to be left in place, it can't be done with a circular saw or jigsaw and even hand tools can't help with what I needed. Being able to easily replace a section of rotting wood on something like a garage door or door frame can pay for the tool alone compared to replacing the entire section of wood.

I was even able to cut down the inside of a door frame from top to bottom along the edge of the molding that the door closes against. Any carpenter would have told me that I would have needed to redo the entire frame for my French doors, and replacing the doors themselves would have been more practical given the same labor. But I was able to fabricate a replacement section using this tool, a router and a table saw.

It really does allow you to cut straight lines in wood freehand. A rotary \\"zip\\" style tool is an example of something that looked great on TV but had limited real life use. If you want to cut out sections of drywall to put in switches, outlets or medicine cabinets, this is the tool to use instead. And you will have no problems doing it freehand. You also have the option of nailing a board inplace temporarily and using it as a guide, since you can literally plunge cut along the edge of it. But you may find that drawing a pencil line works just as well.

I've had a finishing sander for years, and it's handy for tight corners and special needs where no other sander will work. I didn't use it much and didn't think I'd gain much by having yet another tool to do the same thing. But the multifunction tool worked better than the original, and I'd recommend the finger sander as an add on. Having the tool literally already in hand when I needed to sand made me realize how flexible a finishing sander can be and I now use it a lot for that. All it needed was a quick change of attachments.

The stock attachments really do work well for jobs such as stripping linoleum and removing glued down carpet. The only job I found where it did not fully meet expectations was slicing through copper tubing. If you get up above 3/4 inch it will be slow going, and there are better tools for the job unless you need a flush cut and can keep the pipe rigid enough that it won't vibrate independently.
I've even used it to cut slots in screw heads for screwdriver use. Although a Dremel works better for that if you have one already, it's still a good tool for use in a pinch.

The biggest difference between this and other power tools is that there are so many jobs that it not only does well, I can literally think of no alternative short of demolition and replacement. product_title: Milwaukee 49-56-9000 2-1/8-Inch Big Hawg Hole Cutter
review_body: Super fast cutting in soft woods and does well when it hits a nail in the wood with its high speed steel teeth. For Hardie siding or MDF or fiberglass a tungsten carbide tipped hole saw is a lot better (Bosch or Blue Boar) but if all you cut is fir or pine the Hawg cutters cut surprisingly fast.

review_body:

product_title: General Tools & Instruments Cordless Power Precision Electric Screwdriver
review_headline: An Excellent Hard To Find Powered Mini Screwdriver
review_body:
About six years ago I found and bought my first mini powered screwdriver, a brand called the \\"iGo.\\" The iGo was the same in concept as this Ultra Tech in that it was a super mini screwdriver, with small driver bits (albeit the iGo bit are not as small as the Ultra Tech). The iGo is powered by two AAA batteries.

Back then the iGo was the only miniature battery powered screwdriver on the market (at least that I could find). There were plenty of large AA battery powered drivers (that use four batteries), for example Black & Decker's drivers. But those are powerful screwdrivers meant for heavy duty jobs such as inserting wood screws into hardwood.

In 2004, when I was first researching and looking for a battery powered mini screwdriver, I wanted something for delicate, small jobs such as working on computers or small electronic devices. (The Black & Decker type drivers are too big, cumbersome and powerful to work on small screws, plus those powered screwdrivers don't come with bits small enough to fit into small screws.) What size screws am I talking about? Look on your netbook or notebook computer case, to see the screws I am talking about.

Enter the iGo powered screwdriver. Those have served me well all these years and I am still using the original two I bought back then. (Actually, I bought five of them and gave two as gifts. By the way, geeks love these powered mini screwdrivers. My friend gave one to her sister's new husband at their wedding reception, part of a box of gifts. Everyone at the reception was asking to play with the screwdriver and he caught two of his guests trying to \\"forget\\" they had the driver, by putting it in their pockets.

Fast forward to three weeks ago when I decided to see if there were any new powered miniature screwdrivers on the market. A search yielded pay dirt when I found this \\"General Ultra Tech Power Precision Screwdriver\\" (that's a mouthful but that's the official name of it).

I read the description and was impressed that this was obviously a better product than my iGo (even though the iGo was only $5 per driver and it has worked flawlessly). What I liked about this General Ultra Tech is that it comes with six screwdriver bits, including two torx bits (T5 and T6 that typically fit cell phones and small electronics). The bits case has two very small flathead and two small Phillips head bits.

The chuck that the bits fit into are proprietary to the Ultra Tech bits. That means the full size bits that come on bigger drivers won't fit. Besides, bits such as those on a Black & Decker driver are too big to work on small precision screws. And to be sure, a full-sized powered driver would strip screw threads, holes, or heads because there's simply too much power driving the screw.

Sidenote: The iGo driver also has a proprietary chuck and bit. The iGo came with two bits, a flathead and a Phillips, that conveniently stores inside the driver, so you don't lose or misplace them.

Also, the iGo bits and chuck are magnetized, a handy feature when working in tight spaces or difficult to access screw holes. (This General Ultra Tech is not magnetized.)

Impressions of the Ultra tech: This is a great driver. It was a well thought out design and it's perfect for doing precision work.

For example:

-- You grip it like holding a pen. Because it's a small diameter device, you can hold it and easily \\"target\\" the screw you are working with.

-- When using the driver your thumb is conveniently on the power switch. So you can power the switch to screw or unscrew without having to twist or contort your grip to operate the power switch.

-- The driver at the base is curved inward, like many pens that advertise a comfortable grip design. So when holding the driver with your fingers it's really a natural grip.

-- Lastly on the grip or feel in the hand, the driver body is 6\\" long and about the diameter of a U.S. dime. So when holding it, the top half rests on your hand, in between the thumb and forefinger. (This is similar to holding a pen.) This results in your being able to hold the driver firm and steady when using the driver.

All in all, the form factor is a great design and pleasure to use.

Now on performance.

I see some people criticize this as being under powered or incapable of driving certain screws. Excuse me folks, first of all, this is for precision work, not driving bolts or screws into hardwood or metal. This driver has more than enough power to work on any electronic device's screws. If you want more power, trust me, you are going to strip the screw or female threads of whatever you are working on.

True, the driver head has a slight degree of of wobble indicating that these are not machined parts, where tolerances need to be precise.

If the driver contained machined parts these drivers would cost a lot more than $20 to $25. How do I know this? There's a DSLR camera CMOS sensor cleaner that kind of looks the same as this driver, it's a powered pen device that spins fibers at about 10,000 rpm. Those sensor cleaners cost about $100 minimum. Why? Mainly it's because the parts that spin or turn have to be very precise since it will be accessing the insides of a digital camera. The pen obviously contains machined parts and that's why it cost so much. There's some guy on a lathe shaping those precision parts. He has has to be paid.

The Ultra Tech driver is powered by two AAA batteries. I have found on my iGo, because I am not using it that much (maybe 100 times a year) that a set of AAA batteries last me over two years. The driver is still working at that point, but just not as fast or powerful as with a fresh set of batteries.

The package advertises \\"10+ hours of power\\" but I imagine that simply means that if you ran the motor for ten hours while the motor is still technically turning at hour ten, by that time the driver won't work. Obviously, at hour 7 or 8 the driving capabilities are weak or lacking torque (screw turning ability) so it's best to swap out the batteries then and not to wait until the batteries are completely dead.

Bonus Tip: It's best to use rechargeable batteries in devices like this. When you feel that the driver is suffering power loss (getting weaker at driving screws) simply replace the batteries and recharge the old ones. I recommend you get Sanyo's ENELoop rechargeable batteries, by the way. IMHO those are the best rechargeable batteries on the market. (Why? Well for one thing, ENELoop batteries don't discharge much when sitting in a drawer, for example. At least not at the same rate as regular rechargeable batteries.

\\"Screw driving\\"...

I was very impressed. The bits are small for precision screws and detailed work. And the smallest driver bit even fit eyeglass screws!! Now that's a precision, powered screwdriver. What will keep you from doing \\"big jobs\\" with this driver is that the bits are very small, so it can't be used for screws bigger than what you see on your notebook computer, the screws that keep the case together.

Bonus Tip: Do NOT use this screwdriver in powered mode to completely drive in a screw, the driver's motor is too powerful and will strip threads or the screw. When you get close to the where the screw is almost completely screwed in, gently twist the driver to manually finish the job. product_title: Hitachi NR83A & NR83AA Framing Nailer Rebuild Repair Kit
review_body: The title pretty much says it all.  The kit includes all the replacement parts, but it appears to be worth only about 25% of the cost (it consists almost entirely of O-Rings).  Many of the O-Rings are unmarked, so you have to lay them out on a silhouette (provided with the rebuild kit) to figure out the manufacturer's part number.  Then you go to your nail gun instruction manual, and convert the O-Ring manufacturer's part number to the part numbers in the exploded diagram of the user's manual.  If this sounds cumbersome, it is.  Finally, there are no instructions provided with the rebuild kit, and the user's manual that comes with the nailer doesn't include instructions for rebuilding the nailer.  You have to wing it, based on the exploded diagram in the user's manual.  It took me well over two hours to rebuild the gun, and it should have been a relatively easy one hour job.  In summary, the price is too high, and the lack of instructions is unacceptable.  Unfortunately, I don't know of an alternative rebuild kit...

product_title: Inova T4QM-HB Rechargeable 5 Function LED Flashlight
review_headline: Great light, needs a few tweaks.
review_body: The light has a a great range to the beam and the variable brightness and strobe functions are very useful as well. However, I personally feel the light would be better with a couple of changes. There is no eye on the body of the light to thread a lanyard through to hang it off you belt or around your neck if need be. The light has exposed contacts that mate up with the charger which I find a little inconvenient for two reasons. First, you can't charge a battery by itself...you have to have the light in the charger. Secondly, if you work in extremely dirty or oily places as I do, the exposed contacts will get filthy. As with LED lights, when the battery runs out, the light does not dim, it simply shuts off. On the flip side, I bought a second battery and charge both of them before an inspection, then change them out when the battery runs out. The battery advertises two full hours of light and I found that to be very close to my experience with using them. The light is MUCH brighter and MUCH lighter than the one I had been using, so I am very happy overall. When I am going to use it in extreme conditions, I put it in a heavy-duty ziplok bag, taped so the lens is tightly covered, which allows nearly unobstructed light while keeping the switch and contacts clean.

product_title: 55 Gallon Water Preserver Concentrate 5 Year Emergency Disaster Preparedness, Survival Kits, Emergency Water Storage, Earthquake, Hurricane, Safety
review_body:
My order from Acme Prototype via Amazon arrived today stinking strongly of regular everyday chlorine bleach.

The small bottle is packaged with papers in a small zip-lock baggy which was shipped in a small bubble pack mailer and sent via USPS. Which of course got squished somewhere along the way and the contents of the bottle squeezed out all over.

Looking at the active ingredients on the bottle it's Sodium Hypoclorite at 5.25%. Exact same ingredients and concentration used in everyday household bleach. I could have gone to local drug store and bought a couple of gallons for what I was charged for this, plus shipping.

What an absolute ripoff.

Follow up: Acme Prototype imededately shipped out a replacement order, this time in a cardboard box, and refunded my full purchase price for my troubles. Kudos to them for exemplary customer service.

product_title: DEWALT DCF610S2 12-Volt Max 1/4-Inch Screwdriver Kit
review_body:
We are in the midst of major home repairs, so the arrival of this cordless screwdriver came at a very good time. We also let two of the contractors working with us use this machine and it has met with mostly unanimous approval.
We had three minor complaints.
1.The very nice bag it came with has no pockets or sections to keep the battery packs in , so everything just slides around together.
2.It only came with a very small Phillips head bit; granted extra bits can be purchased, but it just seemed that a company with as good of a reputation as DeWalt should at least have included a regular screwdriver bit or even have a reversible one. The one addition I would definitely recommend, is a longer bit than the very little one included, especially to reach into hard to get to places.
3. For a screw driver meant for heavy usage, and why would you be using this if not? It would have been better to have an impact driver; making less strain on your wrist and you do not usually have to drill a pilot hole.

The clutch or torque ring works very well, so that screws are not stripped. Both of our contractors really liked the size of this drill and the light weight of it. It also has a very fast charge for the battery, the first charge to use it only took 30 minutes.
It was a wonder to screw in drapery hardware on molding without splitting the framework and yet was also able to do a heavier job of drilling in screws in a large garden window.
We all loved the LED lights that lit up the area you are working on, that put a smile on everyone's face at the first use.

product_title: PSI Woodworking LR110-3 110-Volt Long Ranger Dust Collector Switch
review_headline: First One Did Not Last Long
review_body: The below was written in November 2010 and now it's July 2011.  The second unit just stopped working.  It's not the relay I added; that works fine when I hard-wire the coil.  I'm sure it's out of warranty so I'll take it apart and see what's happened.  It had worked fine with the setup noted below with intermittent use.  Totally disgusted at this point and can't recommend trying this product.    This product worked great for about two weeks of intermittent use in my home workshop.  The remote faithfully turned on my 1 HP Delta dust collector and it was very cool.  Then, it just stopped working.  The light on the remote still came on but there were no other vital signs.  I changed the battery in the remote and pushed the reset on the unit, because those are the only things I could do without voiding the warranty.  Thankfully, I was still covered under Amazon's warranty and they very promptly shipped me a replacement and I sent them back the dead unit, all at no cost.  But now I didn't trust it.  So I purchased a relay from Graingers rated at 2 HP and wired the relay so that the Long Ranger now just actvates the relay and the relay handles the dust collector's current.  Effectively, I'm using the Long Ranger as a remote actuator and hoping that the first unit's failure would have been avoided if it didn't have to handle the motor's current, although it was rated for up to 1.5 HP.  Or possibly the first unit failed when the second unit would not have.  The relay cost me $29 (side note:  same relay would have been $52 through Amazon, but that's an isolated case) and quite a bit of installation time, but once again everything is cool.

product_title: Quirky SWT-1-CW1 Switch Modular Pocket Knife with 18 Attachments
review_headline: The Swiss Army Knife for the 21st Century
review_body:
The Swiss Army knife, either from [[ASIN:B000QGF986 Victorinox]] or [[ASIN:B001CZDH1Q Wenger]] (Victorinox recently acquired Wenger, but both lines will continue.), is arguably the quintessential pocket tool of the 20th Century, justly celebrated and included on any list of essential pocket items for preparedness in any eventuality, but it isn't perfect. Though Victorinox and Wenger produce dozens of different models, in most cases you will have to settle for something that contains tools you'll never use and something that doesn't contain every tool you'd like to have. (The largest model available: the [[ASIN:B001DZTJRQ Wenger Giant Swiss Army Knife]], which is essentially a dealer demonstrator model of every tool Wenger ever made, now available to the public, is all but unusable.)

Enter the Quirky Switch, the first modular pocket knife, which comes with 18 (NOT 17!) tools, and 3 knife chassis, allowing you to assemble your very own ideal pocket tool. Don't ever drink wine? Then forget the Corkscrew. Work with small steel parts that tend to drop and roll into hard to reach crevices? Then include the Magnet. (Work with magnetic media? Then FORGET the Magnet!) Go through security checks often? Then forget the bladed tools. Then, depending on which tools you choose, select the Small, Medium, or Large knife chassis.

The secret is that the tools are of constant width (or multiples thereof); the Large chassis can hold 22 single-width tools, the Medium chassis can hold 14 single-width tools, and the Small chassis can hold 6 single-width tools. What follows is a detailed list of available tools by width:

Single-Width Tools: Basic Blade, Serrated Blade, Wood Saw, Flathead Screwdriver, Bottle Opener/Large Flathead Screwdriver, Can Opener/Wire Stripper, and Nail File.

Double-Width Tools: Scissors and Magnifying Lens.

Triple-Width Tools: Phillips-Head Screwdriver, Eyeglass Flathead Screwdriver, Eyeglass Phillips-Head Screwdriver, Wrench, and Magnet.

Quadruple-Width Tools: Corkscrew and Tweezers.

Sextuple-Width Tools: Pen and L.E.D. Flashlight.

Defects? There's only one thing that can truly be called a defect: the Corkscrew is wider than its base, causing it to jam against other tools or the side of the chassis. If you take a look at other pocket knives with corkscrews, you will find that most handle the problem of fitting a corkscrew in by putting it on the side and providing a cutout for it. That option isn't available for the Switch so the Corkscrew either needs a Quintuple-Width base or a narrower corkscrew. For now your best bet if you insist on carrying it, is to put the two shortest tools, the Bottle Opener/Flathead Screwdriver and the Can Opener/Wire Stripper on either side of the Corkscrew and hope for the best.

Among the only other issues worth mentioning is that IMHO the bladed tools at least should have fingernail grooves like most pocket knives do. The Switch method of giving every tool a projecting prong for lifting and a hole in the chassis for pushing up from beneath works pretty well, but you don't want to be pushing a bladed tool up from the blade side. Also there is a bit more play in many of the tools when locked open than I'm used to.

All remaining issues can be treated as tradeoffs. Compare a fully loaded Switch chassis with a Swiss Army knife or even an ordinary pocket knife of similar size, and you will find that the Switch holds far fewer tools. That's because the Switch is a \\"single-ender\\" with tools hinged only on one end while most pocket knives are \\"double-enders\\" with tools hinged on both ends interleaving with each other and most Swiss Army knives have a third hinge on the bottom for even more tools. Presumably this was done in order to simplify tool installation, but it does mean you cannot carry as many tools. On the other hand if you've found yourself not using most of the tools on your Swiss Army knife, you may not care.

Second, the full length Switch tools (especially the bladed tools) are only about three quarters as long as they would be on Swiss Army knives or ordinary pocket knives of similar length. That's because all Switch tools fit completely inside the chassis, rather than tapering to a point and extending PAST the opposing hinge. This either matters to you or it doesn't.

Few new products have excited me more, and my mind is bubbling over with suggestions for improvement. First, the Basic Set should include two more pairs of Front and Back Covers, perhaps in different colors, (or they should be sold separately) because there are enough tools in the Basic Set to fill all three chassis if you wanted to set up three pocket tools for differing purposes. Of course not everyone would want to bother, and a given tool could be placed in only one chassis, but the option ought to be there when Quirky takes the obvious next step:

More tools, including replacement/duplicates for the original 18. A Punch or Awl would be a nice to have, as would a USB Memory Stick, maybe a Hex Wrench or two. You can no doubt think of options you'd like to buy. One can even imagine tool sets for specific markets like bicyclists. Carrying pouches, perhaps with belt loops, would be another nice to have.

Single-Width Spacer Rings. In order to make it easier to access tools, especially for someone willing to carry less tools, Single-Width Spacer Rings, essentially Single-Width Tool Bases with everything rounded off would be useful because you will have trouble if you don't fully load your selected chassis. (These would also solve the problem of the defective, too-wide-for-its-base Corkscrew.)

I'm convinced that the Modular Pocket Knife is the wave of the future, but it is more of a question whether the Quirky Switch will be riding that wave. review_body: I am not sure there are any stud finders, especially in this price range, that could ever compete with this one when it comes to ease of use & overall accuracy. product_title: Hitachi 18-volt Lithium-Ion Cordless Impact Driver
review_body: Hitachi makes incredible drill drivers and impact drivers. This is my third Hitachi driver product and I love it. My two other 18v drills have worked flawlessly for more than 3 years and the only reason I bought a second one was because the life of the batteries of the first drill had worn down to nothing. This is normal and totally expected since I use my cordless drills nearly every day as a professional contractor. I finally bought the impact driver because once again I needed new batteries, and I chose the impact driver because I very often need to drive 3 inch course thread screws. Regular driver drills work okay for this but it wears the batteries down quickly and my arms too since you must apply enough continued pressure to keep the bit from slipping in the screw head. This is not a problem at all with a good impact driver, the impact force drives the longest screws into the hardest wood with no problem. This is really the only driver I ever use any more unless I need to use an actuall drill bit. Buy 18v Hitachi drivers and you will be happy. Oh, and they look good too! And I swap my batteries between all my Hitachi drivers without any problem.

product_title: Freeman PFL618BR 3-in-1 Pneumatic Flooring Nailer
review_body: It's not often that I'll actually take the time to write a review but I think this one is worth it. Freeman deserves a pat on the back for this product. I just finished installing about 1,000 sq ft of ¾ inch Brazilian Teak flooring in my house using this gun. I was a bit skeptical at first seeing that the comparable Bostich was more than twice the price and every other gun in the same price range as this one only carried a 1 year warranty. Well, I'm glad I took the chance. At first glance, the fit and finish is was much better than I had expected. The hammer and safety goggles that came with it were also good quality and ended up holding up great. Once I plugged it in and dialed in the right pressure on my compressor, the gun worked perfectly. It had no issues getting through the Teak.    The only advice I would give is to periodically stop and check the hex bolts and tighten them up. Had I done this, I'm certain it wouldn't have jammed on me (It did it twice; both were due to lose bolts, not bad considering I put in over 2000 L Cleats). I'm pretty certain that any piece of equipment getting hit as hard and as many times as I did would've had the same issue. Once everything was tight, it continued to work flawlessly. I would absolutely recommend this to any DIY'er (heck, I think it may even be Pro quality). I know this almost sounds too good to be true, but it really is a good product (7 year warranty too). I will definitely look at Freeman products again if I need any other air tools in the future!

If I am at fault I'll admit it. The instructions call for cutting metal NO THICKER than 1/8 inch. I was in a hurry to try out my new tool and missed reading that part. Tried cutting metal thicker than that and the attachment that turns the cutoff wheel stripped some gears. The main unit was still in great shape. I tried it out on some wood and it worked just great.

I may have also put a little too much pressure on the tool. Again the instructions caution against that. I am an old guy and I don't consider myself as having enough strength to burn out a tool. I did it and I don't consider it the tools fault.

I did get a nice surprise. I contacted Amazon and explained my problem by e-mail. I did not get a return e-mail but today I received a replacement and it was less than 48 hours that I had sent that e-mail. What is even more amazing is that I STILL HAVE THE OLD UNIT. It will be returned as soon as I get an address to return it to. I'm happy they trusted me enough to send me a new unit before i shipped the old one back. Their return e-mail must be stuck in my capricious spam filter.

In my opinion this will be a great LIGHT DUTY tool. Amazon also dropped the price by $70 since I bought it and that makes it an even better deal for any future buyers. If you want a heavier duty tool they do sell one with a higher amperage motor that may cost a bit more.

There are many attachments and blades you can purchse extra for this unit BUT this kit has some very handy attachments already in it. I recommend that you buy this kit first, take a look at what's there, and then decide what extras you'd like to have. Since this kit already has the dust adapter I did go ahead and ordered the vacuum hose that goes between it and the vacuum cleaner.

I also like the fact that the handle can be removed and it has a compartment in it for storing small bits and tools. I have also noticed that the handle has certain slots in it as if there are attachments that fit it also, I'm going to check that out futher.

In conclusion I feel that with the new lower price it makes this kit a deal that is hard to pass up. product_title: Bosch RH328VCQ 1-1/8-Inch SDS Rotary Hammer Kit
review_body: I received this tool and immediately discovered that there was two issues:    1.  A missing depth Gauge    2.  No information about how to acquire the optional 3-jaw chuck - Quote from Product Description on   Amazon:     \\"To save time, a quick-change system provides fast change-outs between an SDS-plus chuck and optional 3-jaw chuck (not included) for use with a wide range of accessories. \\"    I called Bosch about both issues, on my first call I was disconnected during an attempted transfer. I called back and was successfully transferred  and offered a depth Gauge which I had to turn down until they could answer the availability question about the optional 3-jaw chuck. I was transferred once again, only to be told that I needed to be transferred to the tech department at a different number and  they open at 9am central time.  After 9am I called the new phone number and dialed the option that I had been given and was transferred again, at which point the Bosch representative kept questioning if the tool I purchased from Amazon was reconditioned.  I assured them it was new.  Then they next said since its under 30 days that I need to take this up with the seller. I informed them that there own instructions that came with the tool implores the customer to NOT contact the seller but instead contact Bosch with any and all issues, and that going back to the seller would not address the optional 3-jaw chuck question.   Finally I was transferred to a technician that was able to address my question about the availability of the optional 3-jaw chuck.  He said that there is NO optional quick-change 3-jaw chuck specifically for the Bosch RH328VCQ, but that Bosch does make the Bosch 1618571014 SDS-plus Shank 3 Jaw Chuck that fits any Bosch SDS-plus tool regardless of model for around $50.00.   I asked the technician why would I or any customer want to pay the extra $80.00 if the only difference between the Bosch RH328VCQ and the Bosch RH328VC is the quick-change chuck system, ifBosch doesn't make a quick-change 3-jaw chuck?  He acknowledged that consideration and pointed out that there is still value in the quick-change system because SDS chucks wear out and for $58.00 dollars you can keep a spare SDS chuck around and change out a worn SDS chuck in seconds with no down time on the Bosch RH328VCQ.  Where as on the Bosch RH328VC you'd have to send it in for repair.    My conclusion is that while Bosch may make some fine tools they really messed up here and the customer service experience was a big disappointment too.  I found the Milwaukee 5359-21 1-1/8-Inch SDS Drive L-Shape Rotary Hammer on Amazon for $298.99 and called Milwaukee customer service to ask  about a 3 Jaw/SDS Chuck and where the drill is made (Germany same as Bosch) and after one transfer found immediate answers. FYI - The Milwaukee 48-66-1370 SDS/Chuck Adapter Kit sells for $111.10 on Amazon compared with the Bosch 1618571014 SDS-plus Shank 3 Jaw Chuck also on Amazon but for only $41.61 .  After I post this review I'm going to return the Bosch RH328VCQ and order the Milwaukee 5359-21 1-1/8-Inch Rotary Hammer and the Eazypower 30205 1/2-Inch SDS Drill Chuck Adapter 20-UNF Thread for use with a spare keyless 3 Jaw Chuck that I already have.

review_body: There was a time when I preferred not to use gloves when working.  I felt that they were difficult to work with, always in the way. product_title: CT-250 ROTO-SPIN Datacom Jacket stripper. Perfect to Strip Fiber-Optic, Category 5, Datacomm Virtually any Jacketed Cable!
review_body: I have been involved in installing a fire alarm system using a 4 conductor jacketed cable similar to a telephone cable, only using number 18 wire.  It had been installed into standard electrical boxes without stripping the jacket off, and I was concerned on how to strip it without possibly nicking one of the interior wires, as this would be very hard to replace at this point.  I checked out srippers at a couple of local shops, but all that was available, were very expensive, and required a large swing around the wire that was not available to me with the way these cables are installed.  I purchased the roto-spin and it is great.   The adjustment stop is adjustable from a half inch to four inches, but is also removable to allow longer stripping, which was the case in this application.  I am also impressed on how the unit slits the cable jacket all the way down the cable in one application.    The price is right... any downsides?.  The knob holding the adjustment stop is a bit fiddley if one wants to remove the stop for longer cable cuts.  Other than that, the unit really does the trick.

If you are sitting here wondering with irritation what a \\"360 controller\\" is, this is also the tool for you. Automotive fasteners, home electronics, and appliances are no match for your repair skills, and neither are the screws holding those feckless things together.

product_title: GB Electrical SDT6 Circuit Alert 6-in-1 Screwdriver
review_body: I needed to detect electrical cables that are embedded in a wall and live.    I have multimeters (digital and analog) and one of those simple unpowered tester screwdrivers with the illuminating clear handle; all of those need to touch the conductor to function.  So I looked around.   This seemed like the best option.  The blurb claims it can detect voltage without the need to touch the conductors, and comes with audio and visual alerts.  The fact that it doubles as a screwdriver was a side benefit that didn't really influence my decision to buy it.  It requires a battery; I didn't like that, but there was no workaround that would keep me on budget.    So I got to work.  First off I noticed that no matter which bit I used in the tool, it wanted to fall out.  The holder is just a hex hole, without a spring or ball securing widget, so that explains it.  But the simplest multi screwdrivers manage to do this, so the lack of one on this tool is a major failing. I can't understand why it wasn't designed in from the start.    I started to use the tool without a bit.  The shaft is insulated, but because the final half-inch is exposed metal I didn't envisage too much of a lack of sensitivity when trying to detect current.    A few minutes later I found out that the bit is not needed at all.    The tip is extremely sensitive and will flash and beep at the merest hint of electricity.  You'd think that was a good thing, but not so.  Here's what I did to test the tool:    First off, to get a benchmark by detecting a known live circuit that was only separated from the tool by insulation, I placed the tip against the power lead to my computer.  It flashed and beeped rapidly. Great.  That is very clear and audible.    But as I moved the tool away, it kept flashing and beeping. I moved it about, and it stopped.      More testing, so I put the tip against each of these:  - A dead receptacle, with the breaker turned off (but connected to ground).  - A live receptacle, with a device connected and working.  - The plastic cover on a wall-mounted light switch  - An exposed cable, connected but not powered.  - An exposed cable, connected and powered.  - My PC keyboard (USB) by the numlock key.  - My USB mouse cable, next to the mouse.  These last two were scary!  The range of the tool is supposed to be 50-600v, but the maximum power to the USB devices is supposed to be DC, 5v and 100mA at most.  Relatively speaking, that's microscopic.    In every one of the above, the same results.  Lots of flashing and beeping.    The only kind of cable that didn't have a result was one that was not powered and not connected to anything at all.  Hmph.  So, if you want to locate something that could have some kind of electrical connection - but may not actually be working - this will do the job.    I don't think it's wrong to expect the tool to be more useful than that.    On the face of it, then, it's a great idea.  But in practice, it is very poor because it cannot tell the difference between circuits that are live and those that are not.   That is potentially dangerous.    So, as a screwdriver, it fails.  As a tester, it fails.  Don't buy it.

product_title: JET 708359 JWL-1642EVS 16-Inch Swing 42-Inch between Centers 1-1/2 Horsepower Electronic Variable Speed Woodworking Lathe, 115-Volt 1 Phase
review_headline: After three years still a pleasure
review_body:
I bought this lathe to replace a small vintage Sears lathe. I've been turning bowls on it from 6\\" to 16\\" in diameter for about a year. The inverter on this lathe was a key feature because it gave me the most horsepower available given the 110V power in my garage. I am used to inverters and this one is programmed to the max to make turning easy without any fuss. Variable speed by turning a knob (and the rpm display)is only the beginning and there are so many other less visible features such as the automatic speed ramp up, braking, recovery from catches, and reverse that makes it a real winner over multiple pulley and mechanical speed control lathes.

SETUP: Everything was packed well and was intact. I'm neither young nor a strongman but I have experience handling heavy equipment and assembled it myself -- but I do recommend someone to help -- particularly with the headstock. Clean up of packing grease and leveling the legs went smoothly. The bed was true, and the tailstock was aligned with the headstock. As suggested in the manual I built a shelf using 2 x 4's and plywood. Rather than waste the space, I put plywood on both the top and bottom of the 2 x 4 frame, lined it with heavy plastic, and filled the void with 120# of sand. Testing the lathe before and after adding the sand, I found that an out of balance blank could be run about 70 rpm higher with the additional sand before the lathe started vibrating.

USE: With very few minor issues (see below) this lathe just works, and works well. I still get that ineffable pleasure of using a thoughtfully designed and well made machine when I use it.

ISSUES: More power would be nice. It is very easy to quickly rough blanks of cedar and even elm. When you get to hardwoods -- oak and cherry -- cuts have to be much lighter or you get a catch. Given my power situation however, this lathe is the best available.

A minor issue is the tool rest lock which can slip unless youpush hard on the lock. This is only needed when doing hard vibrating work such as roughing or parting at the end of the tool rest where the leverage is maximized.

Last, after a year of use the on-off switch started working intermittently. The flip side of this issue is the great service from Jet. It took one easy phone call to get a free replacement under their warranty.

UPDATE September 2013. Still happy with the lathe and no issues. Someone asked about a revers - yes there is a direction switch. The nice thing about the VFD is you do not have to wait for the spindle to stop turning to put in in reverse. Just flip the switch and the VFD slows the spindle to a stop and then starts the reverse.

product_title: Howard Leight 1030110 Sync Noise-Blocking Stereo Earmuff
review_headline: Great hearing protection, easy to use audio capability
review_body:
I bought the Sync Earmuffs primarily as hearing protection. I wanted hearing protection that would allow me to listen to music while mowing the lawn, and also as regular hearing protection that I could quickly use/remove compared to foam earplugs for jobs around the house with power tools such as saws, sanders, etc.

I considered a pair of regular muffs (with earbuds underneath for mowing), but this product really was perfect for my needs.

Overall construction and look is very nice, no frills but nothing looks or feels cheap or flimsy.

I certainly own better headphones as far as audio reproduction, notably the bass can be pretty thin, and highs can get a little hissy. But honestly when listening over the muted sounds and vibrations of a lawnmower engine 3 feet away from me, I don't really notice the imperfections.

As far as comfort goes, I thought these muffs were really nice, the ear pads are comfortable and head pressure was just right. The headband is padded and comfortable. The ear pads can get a little hot against your skin after you have them on for a couple hours, but the actual ear cups are both padded and vented adequately enough that my ears didn't get irritated or overheat.

In summary, this set works great as hearing protection, and also performs very well as a noise-blocking headphone for the price. I highly recommend for equipment operators or people looking for a noise-blocking audio headset on a budget.

product_title: Makita BMR100W 18-Volt LXT Lithium-Ion Cordless FM/AM Job Site Radio (Tool Only, No Battery)
review_headline: Auxillary 2 input blocked by battery - major design oversight
review_body: [[ASIN:B000V2H7B2 Makita BMR100W 18-Volt LXT Lithium-Ion Cordless FM/AM Job Site Radio]]  While overall a good product, the engineers missed an important requirement to be able to conviently use the 3.5mm auxillary input inside the battery compartment of the unit. This may not be a problem if using the older style batteries which the radio also will accept, but if you are using the 18V Lithium-ion battery, there is no clearence to use a straight cable or regular right angle cable for that matter. I finaly spent over ten dollars to order the lowest profile right angle plug I could locate, and then had to cut the molded shield at a 45 degree angle almost cutting into the wire to actually get it pluged into AUX2 with the Lithium-ion battery installed. I did finally get it to work and there is sufficient room to store an mp3 player inside the battery compartment, but I shouldn't have had to customize a cable make it work.   For this reason I am giving this radio only 3 stars.

product_title: DEWALT DC628K XRP 1-1/4-Inch to 2-1/2-Inch 15-Gauge 34 Degree Angled Finish Nailer
review_headline: Will be at the top of your favorite tool list.
review_body: I've had this gun about 3 years and am still amazed at how great it works. If you take into account what it was designed to do..ie give a dependable,powerful,easy to operate solution to those who don't want the hassle of compressors for small to medium jobs...then it is perfect. The ONLY drawback is the weight and size. But again, as those who own a lot of tools know, there is always some tradeoff, so even considering the weight the tool is perfect. Take the Paslode cordless nailer for instance. It's light and small but you have to buy costly fuel cells, because it's got a mini compression engine in it. As is also apparent in the reviews, the dependability is nowhere near that of this tool.     Those who own lots of tools also know that if a tool is a hassle to use or expensive to use, then after a while you just quit using it. With this Dewalt gun, I keep finding more and more uses for it.  For example I put up a fence without a helper recently. I worked on it for an hour or two at a time, which would be a pain in the neck setting up an air nailer. I used the gun to tack up a section at a time and them come back with screws for actually holding the boards. I used short nails so if I was getting off level I could easily pry boards up and re-position them. Thats just one of the myriad of things you will find yourself using this gun for.    I also recently lent my gun to a buddy who had been reluctant to try it. He was hand nailing trim and even quarter round, which is near impossible to do. I guess he was reluctant because it kinda looks like a toy. I call it my \\"space gun\\". Anyway once he finally used it he fell in love with it. I guess realizing you can work at 5x the speed of hand nailing makes a lightbulb go off. He has one now.    In a nutshell this is my favorite tool and one I would have to immediately repace if it went out.

They are a bit stiff at first and do feel snug around the ears, so they will need to be broken in with repeated use. product_title: Fluke Multimeter
review_body: For the most part, you don't have to think about this meter's limitations, it just works accurately.  It has excellent ergonomics, from the smooth rotary switch, to the ultra-fast bar graph response, to the ultra-fast continuity beep, and the fast autoranging.  All the functions work the way you'd expect them to, and the modes are easy to access with the rotary switch and yellow button.  No complicated menus.  The min/max function captures fast peaks and valleys.  The autohold is very nice for probing around crowded and potentially dangerous spots -- you set it in autohold mode, then you can ignore the meter and look only at your probes.  When the meter senses a good stable voltage reading, it beeps and holds that reading.  Now you can take your probes away and look at your meter again to see what the reading was.

product_title: Makita BDF452 18-Volt LXT Lithium-Ion Cordless 1/2-Inch Driver-Drill Kit
review_body:
Makita has a reputation of building some of the best power tools. This driver/drill won't disappoint. The torque is impressive. The tool is very well balanced to allow you to apply massive amounts of torque very accurately. It's even easy to use left-handed in tight spaces.

The over-torque clutch adjustment works great, and provides a non-clutched \\"drill\\" mode. It's surprising how much faster you can work when you don't have to think about sinking your screw heads too deep.

The nifty LED light on the front is a nice touch (no more chewing on a mini maglite in dark spaces). It turns on automatically during use, and slowly fades out a few seconds after you've stopped the drill.

I just finished a project that required about 150 3-inch deck screws. I pre-drilled every top board, and drove the screws into the bottom board (with the help of a Bosch Clic Change adapter--highly recommended), and the drill performed perfectly. The battery life is amazing.

The included charger is rather impressive on its own. It can recharge a wide range of Makita batteries, and provides a lot of features to extend the effective lifetime of your lithium-ion batteries. (If you haven't done so already, do yourself a favor, and read up on how to take care of lithium-ion cells.)

I was a little worried about runout (I've used expensive drills in the past with terrible runout--bad enough to drill ovals in metal). When I first got the drill, I spun a few jobber drill bits at various speeds with the drill resting on a bench. I couldn't see any runout on mine (I didn't have a dial indicator handy, though). In real-world use, I saw more runout from the cheap, hex-shank drill bits I was using in my chuck adapter than the drill's chuck (the way it should be). My last drill couldn't claim the same level of precision.

I fully intend on buying more LXT-series tools as the need arises.

It seems like a lot of established tool manufacturers are currently banking on their brand recognition and selling poorer-quality tools every year. It's good to see one outfit that refuses to lower the bar just to keep their nearsighted share holders happy.d tool manufacturers are currently banking on their brand recognition and selling poorer-quality tools every year. It's good to see one outfit that refuses to lower the bar just to keep their nearsighted share holders happy.

review_body: This tool kit consists of three basic tools (hammer, screwdriver, and a crescent wrench) as well as a variety of fasteners and hangers.  It would be a good tool kit for a student going off to college or an older person moving into a retirement community.  The floral design limits the appeal to girly-girls, older women, and perhaps men who like flowers. And the fasteners may come in handy.

product_title: Strut Compressor-Parent
review_body: These are well made and worked well.  I used them on two different pair of struts (Dodge Grand Caravan and Mitsubishi Galant).  In both cases, they got the job done and I have no doubt I could do many more before they needed replacing.      Some type of clamp or vice is necessary to hold the strut in place while you compress it.  I clamped the strut in place between two 2x4's held together with a couple clamps (Large C clamps or \\"handy clamps\\").    I will suggest that you consider purchasing two pair.  As another review mentioned, ideally these would be sold in a 3-pack.  When I was working on the Galant, one of the compressors slid around the spring leaving both compressors on the same side.  At no time did it seem they were going to pop off, thanks to the safety pins, but I had to run to my local shop to get another set to pull the far side back together.

product_title: SOG Spirit Fixed Blade / Spear FS01N-CP - Hardcased Black 4.25" Stainles Steel Blade, Removable GRN Handle, Nylon Sheath
review_body: Out of the box this Knife is pretty much as you see it, nothing fancy or glamourous.  There were some complaints I saw regarding the weight of this blade, just my opinion here but I think it's suitably weighted given the function of this blade.      I agree that if you go hunting with the spear, you will get one shot regardless of your skill level with throwing weapons.  If your good, you will hit the animal in the right spot and it will fall right where you hit it... if you suck, you'll either glance off the animal wounding it, or miss it completely.  The Blade features the 'fish hook' design on the back and if your shot penetrated through the skin and not your good enough to drop an animal on the first strike it will probably run off and you'll be chasing it down.      Have no misconceptions though, this this is dangerous tool.  Touch the tip of it when you pull it out of the box and imagine what it would feel like if you dropped it on your foot... that will convince you of it's effectiveness.  For people thinking that this would be a great hunting tool, My native american brothers that occasionally will hunt with spears gave me a valuable piece of advice... use a bow and bring the spear with you.

product_title: Greenlee Communications 4910 SealTite Pro Compression Cable TV "F" Kit wi th KT 8, LC CST, Flaring Tool, SealTite Pro and 10 RG6/RG6Q in Zipper Case
review_headline: Right Tool for the professional looking job!
review_body: I bought this kit along with 250 ft of RG6-Quad cable and a jar of Paladin SealTite RG6-Quad connectors. We were having construction at our house that the cable entry and distribution point was right in the way. I had to for the short term, get it all out of the way of the workers while maintaining TV and Internet. Once they were done with all the work find a new location and run a nice clean set-up.  I consider myself handy but had adone a few Coax patch jobs that clearly prove the right tool for the job is mandatory. I had to do alot of cuts and stripping and crimps and wanted it done right.    This kit allowed good secure and solid connections. Some flakey issues we had before with Cable signals went away once I ran new cable. I've since been able to help relatives with weak TV reception (no cable where they live) by running new lines and solid connectors. The signal strength improved enough to get solid pictures on multiple channels now.    I'm surprised how often i use this kit to create new cables when we relocate TV's in rooms. Don't have to worry about a lot of extra cable    Only slight comment is the depth setting suiggested by Paladin for the crimper is too tight. When I first followed their instructions to the lettter, I created a small metal burr at the end of the connector that can (and did...ouch) easily cause a cut. Backing off the settings a bit solved the problem, just part of the learning curve.

product_title: SKIL 9205-01 8.5 Amp Reciprocating Saw with Variable Speed Dial
review_body:
I bought this as a replacement for a 1965 SKIL Recipro saw that finally gave up the ghost after 40+ years.

My first reaction was - WOW, it's heavy.

I love the ease of blade changing. My antique SKIL required an Allen wrench to change blades.

Two things I miss - The old saw would cut in any of four directions, by loosening and giving
the blade a quarter turn.

The original saw could also be set to cut flush with the base... as in flat on the floor to cut
a clearance in trim molding.

I very much like the new saw's variable speed control system. It's not what I expected, but it seems to work very well.

As you can see, I bought this on impulse - read $$$ - without any research. I was very surprised to see the parent company is Robert Bosch.

First impression is that this is a solid, well-built tool. I need to use it some more and may well want to upgrade my rating.

review_body: I agree with the first reviewer: the knife appears to be very well made but I too was expecting a california legal push button opening knife. The spring has been removed and consequently the knife is very difficult to open. You must press the button and hold down while using your other hand to open the blade which does not have a thumb stud or any indentation in the blade to be able to pull the blade open. I believe the reason for this is because the knife was designed to be a push button opening knife but the spring has been removed almost rendering the knife useless.

product_title: Columbia River Knife and Tool 2850 Bez Tine Skinner Fixed Blade Hunting Knife
review_headline: Best hunting knife I've ever owned
review_body: I've been big game hunting all my life and decided last year I wanted to switch to a fixed blade style since cleaning folding type knives is a pain and the other fixed blade knives I have are too long for gutting (ka-bar fighting and buck special).  I purchased this knife last year and I love it, everyone else that I hunt with had to have one after seeing it in action.     I looked at several different brands and styles that I thought would make good elk/deer gutting and skinning knives.  After handling and getting the feel of several at a local outdoor store I settled on this CRKT knife.    The blade length and shape is perfect for getting up inside the game and the finger grips on the handle are excellent so the knife doesn't slip when \\"wet\\".    Last year I gutted and skinned 2 buck deer and 3 bull elk and the knife was still very sharp.  After last season I gave it 2 passes using my fine grit hone in my lansky sharpening kit set on 25 degree's and it was razor sharp again.    I can't say enough good things about this knife, I can't imagine anyone buying it for this use would be disappointed.

product_title: Makita BCL180W 18-Volt Compact Lithium-Ion Cordless Vacuum Kit
review_body: The  Makita BCL180W Cordless Vacuum Kit is perfect for that quick clean up job. With its light weight, and without any of the bending necessary with most hand-held vacs or of the demands of cords, my injuries are no longer an impediment to the job. The charge holds long enough for me to clean my small home, the battery recharges quickly enough for me, the bag removes and empties easily, i find the design erganomic. I remove the extension for greater suction when needed. Great value for my money. But it's not perfect; there is no "lock" for the power button; i have to keep my finger on it the duration of its use which can tire my hand but then that goes to show the stamina of the battery - it'll outlast me. which, in retrospect, i'm not sure is saying much! but there you have it. And the only way i know the battery is dwindling is when the suction starts to weaken. it would be nice to have an indicator light. Overall, I highly recommend this.  It is now May 2013 and I'm happy to report the vac and all its parts work just as well as the day I bought it 2 and a half years ago. Its convenience and light weight continue to make the quick clean up job the QUICK clean up job. Still love it. But I have one more wish to add to the design - the body needs something that would make it easier to twist open for emptying - something to grip or traction marks.  5/31/2015 - the vac and recharge battery are still working well! So despite its slight shortcomings, for the price I paid and its durability, I just upgraded my review of it to a 5 star rating. Works best on hardwood. It doesn't have the necessary strength to do a good clean job on deep pile carpet.  8/25/16 - still going strong. If it dies on me, I'd get another one.

product_title: Makita BCL180ZW 18-Volt LXT Lithium-Ion Cordless Vacuum (Tool Only, No Battery)
review_body: Received this for Xmas 2010.  As I already have the LXT batteries and a charger, it was a not-too-expensive gift.  This unit has good suction and will clean hard floors well.  The floor attachment is not powered but it'll do a good job on carpeting - I was surprised at the amount of animal hair and dust it was able to pick up.  I use it for quick clean-ups when I'm too lazy to haul out the full sized corded cleaner.  It won't clean as well or thoroughly as a full-sized vacuum, but we're talking about a light battery powered handheld.    Would have been better designed if the power button had a \\"hold\\" feature.  There are times I'll run it for several minutes continuously, and it would be convenient to not have to press in the button all the time.  The unit will require frequent emptying (that's also a compliment, in that this vacuum is capable of taking in a surprising amount of dirt quickly).  I understand the attachment system is nonstandard, but I haven't had a need to use it with other companies' accessories.  At any rate, I doubt the suction it generates is adequate to properly drive a power-brush attachment.  A dusting brush attachment would be handy.    Because the batteries are external and charge quickly, this vacuum is capable of very long (practically unlimited) run-times.  Compared to other cordless handhelds I've had, this one is a winner!  Highly recommended if you're already invested in the LXT battery system.

product_title: MLCS 7733 60-Degree Woodworking Edge Banding Tongue and Groove Set, 1/2-Inch Shank, 2-Piece
review_headline: Excellent quality router bits; recommend long flush trim bit as well
review_body: Overall the bit set performed perfectly!  I purchased this set for edge banding some maple plywood shelves for an entertainment center project.  The bits functioned perfectly and had surprising cutting power, even when being used in a 1.5 hp router table.  There was almost NO tearout from the male end cutting bit in the solid hard maple stock, which says a lot for the anti-kickback and reduced tearout design of the cutters.  The results were similar on quarter sawn stock as well.  The female plywood cutting bit also proved to slice with no burnishing or checking of the plywood surface.  I don't see a real purpose for the bearing on the end of the female cutting bit as the material would have to be over an inch thick in order to need it when centered in the workpiece.  Instead I was meticulous about the table fence spacing leading and trailing the cutter.    Gluing and clamping was a breeze, although I recommend using a slice of a scrap piece of wood that has been passed through the male end cutter for spreading and evening out the glue once applied to the groove.   I intentionally started with a thicker stock of banding material so that there is a little lip once it's joined.  Once I did that, I was able to take a flush trim bit with the bearing at the end and use it to shave the excess along with beaded glue right off.    The end result is very professional looking and results in a resilience to warping later on, in addition to the aesthetic improvement.

product_title: 10ft (3M) K type Thermocouple with 8cm pole (waterproof)
review_headline: This thermocouple works well for a Sous Vide Controller, up to a point
review_body: I bought this thermocouple to use with a [[ASIN:B002PIM3R8 Dual Digital Display PID Temperature Controller. Ideal for FURNACE & KILN control]] to make a sous vide controller. I set the PID to use a K type thermocouple. At first the thermocouple did not seem to work at all well, any particular temperature read a particular temperature on the front panel readout of the PID, so it could hold a temperature in the water bath just fine, but when I changed the temperature a few degrees on the front panel, the water bath would change temperature in response to the PID's control, and the thermocouple readout changed by some number of degrees that differed from the change as measured by two thermometers I had (which tracked with each other).  In other words, you would get the offset to where it was right on at 135, but 140 might be 143 and 146 might be 144.  The PID allows you to set an offset, but it is a single offset and when I had it reading with my thermometer, a temperature 10 degrees away might be 5 degrees different than my readout.    I wrote a note to the company, and they responded with a couple of suggestions, and also noted that if I could not get it working that I should return it on Amazon for replacement.  So they were supporting it and standing behind it.    I then tried one of their suggestions which involved reversing the leads, and that didn't work, the thermocouple indication went down as the water warmed. When I reconnected it to use it that night, figuring I'd set the water temp with a thermometer and then the PID would hold it, and I could ignore the indication, I found that it was now tracking with my thermometer.    So, why is this a four star rating and not a five, now that it is working?  Well, I was also informed by the company that this is not a waterproof thermocouple. The probe cover is stainless, that makes the probe tip waterproof, but the connection from the thermocouple to the braided cover (where the spring goes) is not waterproof.  If water gets in there, it could cause the symptoms I saw.  What I got was the probe, spring strain relief on the probe end, and wire - the other pictured item, which I presume was some sort of bulkhead crossing device and which I was hoping to permanently mount on a rice cooker, was not packaged with the thermocouple.    I can stick the thermocouple through the grommet in the lid of my rice cooker, which works fine. But trying to use it with my roaster gives me just too much of a chance of the thermocouple slipping and dunking into my water, making the thermocouple inaccurate.    So this seems to be a waterproof probe thermocouple, not a waterproof thermocouple.  The steel cable seems to want to kink.  I am going to put together another controller and this time I will use a [[ASIN:B0052IGFZ4 Waterproof PT100 RTD Thermocouple for PID Temperature Controller (2M)]], it is stronger, it has a plastic coat that goes way up the shaft, and it is only six feet long, which is plenty. Also, people say that the PT100 is more likely to be stable because the third lead allows for some sort of stabilization, I don't understand it but, well, I will try it.

product_title: Empire Level 419-48 Heavy Duty Adjustable Drywall T-Square
review_body:
Works good, what more can I say? The notch to lock the square at 90 degrees is accurate, and it easily adjusts and locks to any required angle. It is surprisingly stout, with the metal being probably 1/4 inch thick. The ruler marks are easy enough to read, and accurate.

Edit: This was a real time-saver recently, when we had to replace some odd-shaped roof panels. One side of the roof was cut at an angle, and instead of using protractors, or complicated math, we just used this square. We snapped a straight start line, held one edge of the square against that, and rotated the other leg of the square to match the angled edge. Tightening up the knob locked it in place, and we had the precise angle for marking the next panel for cutting. Instead of several minutes of figuring, we instead had a 10 second job of hold, align, lock, and mark. The only caution I might give, is that there are 'notches' that lock the legs at a right angle to each other (90 degrees) and if you try to lock it at an angle very close to that, it will tend to fall into the notches, to form a right angle. I'd say it works really well on any angle that is less than 80 or more than 100 degree bend or so. Another nice touch is that the bolt that holds the locking mechanism is recessed to be flush to the backside of the square, so there are no odd protrusions to catch on things or bolt head to scratch delicate surfaces.
The markings are still clear, and easy to read. I would raise this to 4 1/2 or maybe even to 5 stars in usefulness, considering how much time we saved using it to establish the cutting angle on the aforementioned panels.

product_title: SE JT63055 Watchband Link Pin Remover
review_body: Pros:   1. The adjustable bed helps to ensure proper alignment and thus prevent possible tool breakage.  2. The Pin Pusher screw is removable so you can use it to remove Spring Bars or drive pins back into links with a wee hammer.  3. It works and it's cheap. Resized my Fossil PR-5332 with ease.  4. The transverse slot (perpendicular to the Pin Pusher) can be used to securely hold your watch band while you hammer the pins back into the band links.    Cons:    1. This is not a precision swiss watch tool.  2. The screw system is made of plastic with very loose tolerances, which translates into significant Pusher Pin wobble.  3. An ALL-metal version with machine screw threads would do a better job, but I haven't seen such a thing with an adjustable bed.    TIPS!!  Wrap the body/case of your watch with a strip of soft cotton cloth and use sticky tape around the cloth to hold it in place. This will protect the case, bezel & crystal from scratches.    Have a parts tray handy! Do NOT loose parts! Muffin baking tin is good.    Use magnifier lamp or mag-goggles if you have 'em.    A good strong sturdy wood/steel workbench is best, because it doesn't bend/bounce under your tool when you try to hammer pins back in.    A small piece of hard plastic to use as a punch when hammering pins back in can protect the band from damage, but you'll need to use the Pin Pusher to recess the link pins.

product_title: DELTA 36-136 Universal Miter Saw Stand
review_body: I used this stand for one project (3000sf framing, detached garage and siding) and became very frustrated with it by the end of the job.  The stand itself is generally well constructed, and once set up is a pretty good and stable stand. Problem is, its doesn't break down and set up well or quickly, and constant loading and unloading from the tool trailer began to wear the mounting hardware quickly.  I had my DeWalt 12\\" slider mounted to this stand and the weight of the saw was too much for the mounting hardware causing it to loosen quickly and constantly and go out of alignment with the outfeed arms(I do think I should have mounted the saw to a piece of plywood and then mounted the plywood to the stand).  The mounting hardware was constntly being retightened and resulted in stripping the allen heads.  The outfeed arms sag, and don't set up at the same height after break down and set up.  The sag in the arms differs by the distance extended. The results are having to adjust the height on the rollers every time you move the out feed arms and the mechanism for doing this is slow. I always felt like I needed to over tighten the knobs for the arms and rollers but was nervouse after stripping the mounting hardware.  Also, the stand is heavy and long and as with all the wheeled stands ive used, moving around and navigating through doorways is cumbersome.  Lastly, and really the biggest setback now that I think about it is, your saw is permanently mounted to the stand and there is NO option for quickly removing your saw if you need to get this up stairs or in tight places or store it or use multiple saws on one stand.  I can compare this stand to the following which I own or have owned:  DeWalt, which is very easy to set up, not portable with the saw attached, but solid and consistent and remains in the tool trailer for framing, decks and siding projects.  Ridgid MSUV, very easy to set up, maneuverable (though does require partial breakdown to move), easily remove saw fromstand, pretty cool outfeed supports, very heavy and not built well. This stand lasted a little longer than the Delta. I gave it to a friend.  And the Bosch Gravity Rise, the all around best stand, tough, reliable, saw is removable and set up is consistent. I use this for all interior remodel work and trim outs.  For shop use or for a homeowner who is going to set the stand up once in a while, or leave it set up in the shop and just use it to move the saw around, I would say buy with NO hesitation.  If you're a professional contractor or any subtrade, consider a different stand.

review_headline: Legos for your garage . . . Get the clutter off the floor!

The fixtures that attach to the wall are \\"wall docks\\" and you then hang the various hooks and racks on the docks, and your gear off the hooks. The hooks/racks are removable via pushing the red button. I have been hanging garage stuff off hooks screwed into walls for a long time, but the difference here is: 1) These look professional and tidy; 2) You can pop off the racks and hooks and move them to other docks located elsewhere in the garage.

As a life long pack rat, I have always needed to figure out the best way to store my stuff. The key is separating out \\"frequent use\\" from \\"rare use\\" and storing accordingly. Easy access is a must for frequently used items. The beauty of this system is that after you get your stuff off the garage floor, you can rotate your stuff from dock to dock by season. The racks I use for biking with the kids is positioned near the garage door during the summer. During the winter, when it is too cold and dark in the late afternoon to go biking, I change those racks to the rear, harder to access portion of my garage. The docks are light weight and made of plastic, so I probably won't be hanging really heavy stuff from them, but for basic garage clutter, like bikes, hoses, garden tools, etc, this is a well-designed, economical solution that is unique because of the ability to swap out racks/hooks from one dock to another.

product_title: 1.5-Inch Rotary Hammer Drill Three Function Combo, Hammer, Drill Tool
review_headline: Cheaper to buy this than rent one, but read this regarding the chuck
review_body:
This tool drills through concrete faster than my cordless drill puts holes through pine. It's a good quality, low priced import. I'm a homeowner who needed to drill a bunch of mounting holes through concrete, and had no problems using this drill with SDS drill bits. SDS is a snap-in chuck system with grooves and slots so that the drill or chisel bits can not slip.

However, watch out for the auxiliary chuck. This has an SDS shank to attach it to the drill, so you can use smaller round or hex shank drill bits. The problem is, this drill is too powerful for use with small, round profile drill bits. These can slip no matter how tightly you clamp them down. Also, some round shank masonry bits have a half-circle profile on the back end. If this gets caught in the reverse-thread phillips head screw that connects the shank to the chuck, and the bit slips, it will unscrew the screw and the chuck will split. I'm speaking from experience...I went out and bought an SDS drill bit to finish the job.

Summary: drills through concrete like soft wood, but use SDS bits!

I did get a superior polished finish that rivaled the factory edges with most of my 90 degree cuts, but the thin blade tended to flex and \\"walk\\" when attempting to cut off less than 1/8 inch and especially when cutting with the blade at a 45 degree angle. In my experience, it was definitely not like a \\"hot knife through butter\\" as another reviewer suggested.  I don't recycle water and I usually draw the blade through the tile at a slow, even pace to get the smoothest cut possible. review_body:
